When this was done, the soul became very joyful and began to work in this new power, celebrating the wonders of God with praise. It thought that from then on, it would walk continually in that same light, strength, and joy. But it was soon attacked: from the *outside* by the shame and reproach of the world, and from *within* by great temptation, so that it began to doubt whether its foundation <note>original: "Ground"</note> was truly from God, and whether it had really shared in His grace. For the accuser, Satan, came to it and wanted <note>original: "would fain"</note> to lead it away from this path, making it doubt whether this was the true way. He whispered inwardly, "*This happy change in your spirit is not from God, but only from your own imagination.*" The divine light also withdrew into the soul and shone only in its innermost depths <note>original: "inward Ground"</note>, like fire buried under embers, so that reason was perplexed and thought itself forsaken. The soul did not understand what had happened to it, nor whether it had really and truly tasted of the heavenly gift or not. 

Yet it could not stop struggling, for the burning fire of love had been planted within it, creating an intense and constant hunger and thirst for divine sweetness. So, at length, it began to pray properly, to humble itself in the presence of God, and to examine and test its evil inclinations and thoughts in order to put them away. By this means, the will of reason was broken, and the evil inclinations inherent in it were killed and rooted out <note>original: "extirpated"</note> more and more. This process was very severe and painful to the physical body, for it made it faint and weak, as if it had been very sick. Yet it was no natural sickness, but only the sorrow <note>original: "Melancholy"</note> of its earthly nature, feeling and mourning the destruction of its evil desires <note>original: "Lusts"</note>.

Now, when earthly reason found itself thus forsaken, and the poor soul saw that it was despised externally and mocked by the world because it would no longer walk in the way of wickedness and vanity—and also that it was inwardly attacked by the accuser, Satan, who mocked it and constantly presented the beauty, riches, and glory of the world to it, calling it a fool for not embracing them—it began to think and say this within itself:

> O eternal God! What shall I do now to find rest?

### *The enlightened soul met it again and spoke to it.*

While it was in this consideration, the enlightened soul met with it again and said, "What is troubling you, my brother, that you are so heavy-hearted and sad?"

### *The distressed soul said,*

"I have followed your advice and thereby reached a ray or an outpouring <note>original: "Emanation"</note> of divine sweetness, but it has left me again, and I am now deserted. Furthermore, I face great trials and afflictions in the world, for all my good friends forsake and scorn me. I am also inwardly attacked with anguish and doubt, and I do not know what to do."

### *The enlightened soul said,*

"Now I like your condition very much; for now our beloved Lord Jesus Christ is performing that same earthly pilgrimage or process <note>the soul's journey is compared to the life and suffering of Christ</note> with you and within you that He did Himself when He was in this world. He was constantly reviled, despised, and slandered, and owned nothing in this world; now you bear His mark or badge. Do not be surprised by this or think it strange, for it must be so in order that you may be tested, refined, and purified. In this anguish and distress, you will naturally hunger and cry out for deliverance; through such hunger and prayer, you will attract grace to yourself both from within and from without. For you must grow from above and from beneath to be the—

For through that agitation, the power of the sun <note>original: "Virtue of the Sun"</note> moves in the plant, whereby its wild properties become penetrated and infused <note>original: "tinctured"</note> with the solar power, and it grows by that means.

In this way, out of fire and light (that is, wrath and love), there comes to be one essence, being, or substance, which is the true temple of God. Therefore, do not be frightened <note>original: "dismayed"</note> by the temptations of the Devil, who seeks and fights for the kingdom which he once had in you; but, having now lost it, he must be frustrated <note>original: "confounded"</note> and depart from you. He covers you outwardly with the shame and criticism <note>original: "Reproach"</note> of the world so that his own shame may not be known, and so that you may be hidden from the world. For with your New Birth or regenerated nature, you are in the Divine Harmony in Heaven. Be patient, therefore, and wait upon the Lord; and whatever shall happen to you, take it all from his hands, as intended by him for your highest good. And so the enlightened soul departed from it.

### *The Distressed Soul’s Course.*

The distressed soul began its course now under the patient suffering of Christ; and depending solely upon the strength and power of God within it, it entered into hope. From then on, it grew stronger every day, and its evil inclinations died more and more within it. So it arrived at length to a high state or degree of grace; and the gates of the Divine Revelation and the Kingdom of Heaven were opened to and revealed <note>original: "manifested"</note> in it.

And thus the soul, through repentance, faith, and prayer, returned to its original and true rest, and became a proper and beloved child of God again; to which may he, of his infinite mercy, help us all. *Amen.*

# TO THE READER.

<image-desc>A large decorative drop-cap 'T' set within a square woodcut border. The border features ornate floral patterns, scrollwork, and circular motifs.</image-desc>

**T**HIS useful and instructive treatise by the blessed Behmen <note>original: "Behmen"; Jacob Boehme (1575–1624), a famous German Christian mystic and theologian</note> on *The Four Complexions* <note>original: "Complexions"; in early modern medicine, this refers to a person's temperament or the balance of their bodily "humors"</note> is very appropriately attached to the preceding description of *The Way to Christ*. For the foundation of the Christianity taught there is laid in such a deep and earnest exercise of repentance that it shakes the soul of the natural man to its core. By that shock <note>original: "Concussion"</note>, it stirs up and brings to his view the foul dregs of corruption that have previously lain there undisturbed. The horror of this sight, along with the painful sense of guilt and misery that follows it—which the author calls the "Judgment of the Soul or Conscience"—proves to be a very severe trial to the young soldier of Christ at his first entrance into spiritual warfare. In some instances, it is a *long* as well as a sharp process. It may continue for many years, as J.B. <note>Jacob Boehme</note> says in *The Book of Repentance*, if he does not earnestly and quickly put on the armor of Christ. This is a very deplorable condition indeed, and it sometimes occurs among us even today. But it happens in no one so frequently as in souls surrounded by a melancholy temperament <note>original: "melancholy Complexion"</note>—especially if they have defiled themselves with many gross sins, or have adopted mistaken ideas that they were originally rejected <note>original: "reprobated"</note> by God or have out-sinned their day of grace.

This extreme spiritual distress—the poignant anguish and bitterness of which no one can understand unless they have felt it themselves—finds a friendly relief here. Every piece of information is shared, every advice given, and every consolation administered that this unhappy case could require, short of the immediate intervention of the Great and only sufficient Comforter <note>The Holy Spirit</note> himself. The way for His joyful entrance into the afflicted soul is opened and cleared here by removing all those doubts and fears. These fears arise from the soul’s ignorance of its own true nature and essence, and its necessary subjection—while living in the body—to the influence of the astral powers <note>The perceived influence of the stars and planets on human nature and physical health</note> and its own natural temperament. This beneficial knowledge is fundamentally, though briefly, revealed in the following short treatise. It comes from such a divine basis and authority, and with such satisfying fullness and conviction, that it leaves no doubt of its truth or worth. This treatise is, as noted at the start of the last chapter, *An Universal Mirror* or *Looking-Glass wherein every soul may see itself*. It was written exactly as it was represented by the light of God’s Spirit to the *spiritual understanding* of the author.

<keywords>Jacob Boehme, The Four Complexions, spiritual warfare, repentance, melancholy, astral influence, Christian mysticism, temperament</keywords>

->The First Chapter.<-

## Concerning the Cause of Spiritual Trouble, Sadness, and Fear; and the Nature and Origin of such Disturbance, Anxiety, and Fear.

1. <margin>A</margin> All sorrow, anguish, and fear regarding spiritual matters, by which a person is dejected and terrified within themselves, proceeds from the soul. For the outward spirit—which originates from the constellations and elements—is not disturbed or perplexed in this way, because it lives within its own "mother" <note>original: "Mother"; Boehme uses this term to refer to the source or natural matrix from which something is born</note> from which it was born.

2. But because of the heavy fall of Adam, the poor soul has entered into a strange inn or lodging—specifically, into the spirit of this world, which is not its proper home. Through this, that originally beautiful creature <note>meaning the soul</note> is obscured and defaced, and is also held captive there as if in a dark prison or dungeon.

3. Now this strange inn, the spirit of this world, has four "chambers" in which the soul—that noble jewel—is confined. Of these four, only one is primarily manifested in every individual and dominates their life. It is just like the four elements <note>earth, air, fire, and water</note>, which every person contains and is actually composed of; all of them, that is, except the soul, which is not made of that elementary substance, even though it is imprisoned and held captive within it.

4. These four chambers of the soul—or "complexions" <term>Complexion: In pre-modern medicine and psychology, this refers to the temperament or personality type resulting from the balance of bodily fluids or "humors."</term>, as they are commonly called—are:

->1. The CHOLERIC.<-
->2. The SANGUINE.<-
->3. The PHLEGMATIC.<-
->4. The MELANCHOLY.<-

## I. Regarding the Choleric Complexion.

5. The choleric complexion has the properties of fire. It produces violent anger, bold courage, aspiring pride, strong self-confidence, and a disregard for all other people.

6. In terms of the outward world, this form or complexion appears as a fiery light. It longs and labors for the power of the sun and always desires to be lord and master.

## II. Of the Sanguine

**7. The Sanguine** complexion <note>original: "S A N G U I N E"</note>, which has its nature according to the element of air, is subtle, friendly, and cheerful, but not of a firm and resolute mind. It is fickle and easily moved from one thing to another. It readily receives into its essence the property and inclination of the stars. It is naturally chaste, modest, and pure. Through its searching skill and knowledge, it is capable of reaching and mastering great mysteries.

## III. Of the Phlegmatic

**8. The Phlegmatic** <note>original: "P H L E G M A T I C K"</note> complexion takes after the nature of its corresponding element in the outward world: water. It is apt to be heavy, coarse, soft, and yielding. it produces a weak and effeminate mind with a dull apprehension, though it is retentive of what it has once learned. Knowledge must be brought into it through much teaching and repetition from the outside, for it does not find knowledge in its own root. It generally lets all trouble slide off and pass by, and does not burden itself with many cares. It has a glimpse of the light; as for its temper, it is neither sad nor merry, but rather even and indifferent.

## IV. Of the Melancholy

**9. The Melancholy** <note>original: "M E L A N C H O L Y"</note> complexion partakes of the property of the earth. Like the earth, it is cold, hard, dark, and hungry for light. Moreover, it stands in continual fear of the anger of God.

**10.** This is because the earth and stones are on the outside of the "Eternal Essentiality." They are substances solidified through the kindled desire in the *Fiat* <note>Latin: "Let it be done," referring to the divine command of creation.</note>, according to both the property of anger and the property of love. There is both good and evil in their composition.

**11.** However, the good and evil stand in perpetual opposition to each other. For this reason, the good always tries to fly from the evil. This can be seen in metals, where the tincture <term>In alchemy and Boehme’s philosophy, the "tincture" refers to the spiritual essence, inner life-force, or light of a substance.</term> is good, but the total mass or earthly body is evil and wrathful. In metals, the tincture always tries to fly from the earthly part and separate itself from it, especially when the evil constellation or starry influence stirs it. This is the cause and basis for the growth of metals. The tincture drives their desire forth from itself and seeks to fly away from it; however, in its desire, it acquires such a corporeality or substance as the spirit or desire itself is. This is how the metallic body is produced.

**12. The Melancholy nature** is dark and dry. It yields little substance or corporeality in itself, but corrodes and consumes itself inwardly in its own being. It remains always in the house of sorrow and sadness. Even when the sun shines into it, it remains sad within itself. It does receive some light and refreshment from the sun’s luster and influence, but in the dark, it is ever in fear and terror of God’s judgment.

**13.** Now, if any one of these complexions predominates in a person so that it is their specific complexion, then their "noble jewel"—the soul—stands in that "house." During its life in the body, if the soul does not fully attain the light of God within itself, it must help itself with the light of the sun. This is because in Adam, the divine "Light-Eye" <note>The eye of spiritual perception or the "eye of the soul."</note> became shut to the soul when it entered the earthly source or property.

**14. The soul** in Adam did admit into itself the outward complexions: the spirit of the macrocosm <note>original: "Great World"</note>, the stars, and the elements. Because of this, it has now come to pass that

# Chapter 1. A Treatise of the Four Temperaments <note>original: "Complexions"</note>.

In this lifetime, these dwell within one another: the soul in the temperaments, and they in the soul. Yet, one does not contain the other in its essence. The soul is deeper than the outward spirit, but during this life, they cling to each other just as the inward and outward worlds do; although one is not the other, the outward spirit is not the soul.

15. In its first essence and proper substance, the soul is a magical fire-source or property, originating from God the Father’s nature. It is an intense and unceasing desire for the Light—just as God the Father, with intense desire from eternity to eternity, always desires His Heart (that is, the center of the Light) and generates it through His desiring will out of the fire's property. We see this naturally, as light is generated out of fire.

16. But no fire can exist unless it has a root or ground for its existence; this ground is the Center of Nature. The soul also has this within itself, burning forth from the forms of nature—specifically, from the Dark World. In its property of desire, this world drives itself forward until it reaches the fire, and then it desires freedom—the Light—as is explained at length in the book *The Threefold Life*.

17. Therefore, since the soul is a hungry, magical fire-spirit, it desires spiritual substance <note>original: "Substantiality"</note> or virtue to sustain and preserve its fire-life, and to soften or soothe the raging hunger of its fire-quality.

18. Now it is well known—and painfully felt—how the soul, through **Adam** in his disobedience, entered into the spirit of this world and ate from it. Therefore, **Christ** became a man in our essence so that He might bring the soul back again, through the center and through God’s fire, into His Light—the World of Meekness. This was actually achieved in the person and process of Christ.

19. Since the hungry soul is already involved in the spirit of the "Great World" <note>the macrocosm or physical universe</note> within the temperaments from the mother's womb, it eats from the spirit of this world immediately from birth, and even while still in the womb.

20. The soul eats spiritual food—namely, from the spirit of the forms or qualities of the temperaments. It does not eat their entire essence, but acts magically; it is like the igniting of their fire. The temperament <note>original: "Complexion"</note> becomes like the soul in the soul's fire. The two are like fuel and fire to each other: understand the temperament as the fuel and the soul as the fire.

21. Now, the fire must have fuel, which must be either the outward temperament or a divine substance from God’s own being. It must eat one of these, or perish. But it is impossible for it to perish because it is a "Desire." Wherever there is a desire, there is also an essence or being; the desire creates this for itself.

22. Thus, we may understand the cause of the infinite variety in human wills and actions. Whatever the soul eats, and whatever ignites its fire-life, determines how that soul’s life is led and governed.

23. If the soul leaves its temperament and enters God’s love-fire—the heavenly substance which is **Christ’s** embodiment <note>original: "Corporeity"</note> according to the angelic Light-World—then it eats of **Christ’s** flesh. This is His heavenly flesh, or eternal substance: the gentleness <note>original: "Meekness"</note> of the light of His Majesty. In this, the fire of God the Father creates a tincture <note>a spiritual essence or transforming power</note> within the brilliance of the light.

24. The soul’s fire feeds upon that substance in the water-source or fountain of eternal life, about which **Christ** said He would give us such water to drink. This is the divine, heavenly substance which, through the tincture, is transformed into heavenly spiritual blood.

It describes Christ's role in providing heavenly substance as "food" to redirect the soul from its worldly hunger back toward God's light.</summary>

25. From there, the soul gains a divine will and leads the body to do what it would not do according to its own natural inclination and the "spirit of this world." In such a soul, the <term>complexion</term> <note>In Early Modern psychology, the "complexion" refers to the specific balance of the four humors—phlegm, blood, yellow bile, and black bile—which determined a person's natural temperament and physical health.</note> does not rule; instead, it remains only in the lower, fleshly nature and carries influence only over the outward body.

26. Such a person seeks God's Word and has a continual longing for God. Their inward desire is always to speak of God and to taste more and more of his sweetness; however, this desire is constantly covered and hindered by their natural temperament. Thus, they live in a continual conflict. The soul strives against the temperament, and the temperament against the soul, for they are now tied together in one bond. The temperament is always seeking to enter into the soul's fire and ignite itself with it so that it might obtain full life through it.

27. For when the soul partakes of God's inward, living Word, the temperament—as far as its power of acting is concerned—is suppressed and captivated, though it remains a living principle in itself. But the soul is so faithful in the presence of God's love (which is the only help it has in this combat) that often, when it partakes of his "love-essence," it brings an exulting triumph and divine taste into the temperament itself. Because of this, the whole body is affected and even trembles for joy, being raised to such a degree of divine sensation that it feels as if it were on the very borders of Paradise.

28. But this rapturous state rarely continues for long. The soul is soon clouded or obscured by something of another nature, which is introduced into the temperament through the outward imagination from the "spirit of the great world" <note>original: "Spirit of the great World"; the macrocosm or the external universe, which was believed to influence the human "microcosm" through the stars and elements.</note>. The soul makes a mirror of this influence and begins to contemplate it with its outward imagination. In this way, it wanders away from the Spirit of God and is often stuck in the "dirt" <note>meaning worldly filth or sin</note> unless the Virgin of Divine Wisdom <note>original: "Virgin of Divine Wisdom"; a personification of the Sophia, or the pure, divine insight that reflects God's light.</note> calls it back again to repent and return to its first love. This danger is pointed out here and set before the soul as a warning to be careful of its ways.

29. For when the soul focuses its imagination on or according to its natural temperament—and so partakes of it and turns itself away from God's Word and Will—it follows the guidance and acts according to the property and inclination of that temperament. It receives everything that is injected from the <term>constellation</term> <note>The perceived influence of the stars and planets on human behavior and destiny.</note> or the power of the stars into the temperament, or whatever is introduced into it through its imagination from the spirit of the external world. It poisons itself through the desire in the temperament with all outward things or substances, and with everything done in the world by either words or actions. The desire of the temperament brings such matter as fuel into the soul’s fire, and the fire is fed and kept alive by it.

30. Here we find how it is that all evil works burn in the fire of God the Father, in which the soul stands or has its life. Whatever is not agreeable or compatible with the love of God, that love cannot receive.

31. Here too we find what sin is, how it works, and how God becomes "angry." It happens like this: when an "abomination" <note>meaning a great sin or spiritual impurity</note> committed by a person is introduced into the burning ground or life of the soul, it withholds the soul from God's love and makes its fire totally dark and blind to his wisdom and light.

32. For the Spirit of God does not enter into the burning fire or life of the abomination, nor does it rise in the center of the soul until the soul leaves the abomination and washes itself anew in the water of eternal life through earnest repentance. Then, indeed, it becomes renewed again in the fire of God's meekness and in the Holy Spirit, like a new child; it begins again to drink of that water and at length recovers its former life in God.

## The Second Chapter.

### *Of the Four <term>Complexions</term> individually, with their respective properties; what the soul and the whole man does, and how they are driven when the soul kindles its fire-life merely from the temperament and the influence of the stars.*
<note>original: "Complexions". In early modern medicine and psychology, a 'complexion' or 'temperament' referred to the balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which were believed to determine a person's physical health and character.</note>

#### I. Of the <term>CHOLERIC</term> COMPLEXION.
<note>original: "CHOLERICK". The choleric temperament was associated with yellow bile and the element of fire; it was characterized by ambition, energy, and a quick temper.</note>

33. If the soul's life is clothed or encompassed by the *choleric temperament*, then it is fiery, fierce, wrathful, ambitious, and fretful. It also provides a body with a form and temper matching itself: thin, unattractive, sharp, and subject to anger. And if the soul focuses its imagination into or according to this temperament, it inflames the temperament even more vehemently, as the soul itself is of a fiery origin and nature.

34. Then anger, pride, ambition, or a desire for exaltation in power and greatness rise up and work in that man. He feels a will to tread everyone underfoot, to despise and insult the poor and miserable, and to tyrannize over those who are subject to him. He would not even care if he committed murder in his anger, were it not that the <term>constellation</term> or influence of the stars hindered it; these often unite with the temperament, inject something into the mind, and prevent much mischief.
<note>original: "Constellation". Early modern thinkers believed the alignment of the stars at birth directly influenced a person's character and destiny.</note>

35. There is great danger in this temperament if the soul lives according to the outward imagination. The bond or knot is harder to break through because one fire-source or property is thus bound or linked to another: the fire-essence of the temperament to the fire-essence of the soul. The fierce, wrathful Devil likewise has a free and powerful access to this temperament, for the fiery property is open and subject to him. He also is proud, stately, and envious, just like this temperament.

36. O, how hardly will the soul be loosed or freed once it is thoroughly kindled and inflamed in this property! The Devil does not even need to tempt it, for it dances along very willingly to his tune.

37. It is not apt to be sad or sorrowful because it has a "fire-light" within its temperament, which it always supposes to be the Divine Light. It believes that by walking according to this light, it walks in the right way; yet it is nothing better than a proud, envious, wrathful, violent, imperious, and oppressive "will-spirit," as long as it is inspired only by its temperament.

38. It indeed makes a grand show with the luster of its fiery temperament, and in its great pride and deep hypocrisy, it would gladly pass for holy. But, O you devil in the form of an angel, how horribly dark you are when the fire-light of your temperament goes out at your separation from the body!

#### II. Of the <term>SANGUINE</term> COMPLEXION.
<note>original: "SANGUINE". The sanguine temperament was associated with blood and the element of air; it was characterized by a cheerful, social, and optimistic nature.</note>

39. The sanguine temperament is meek, gentle, bright, and cheerful, according to the property of the element of Air. It is imaginative, courteous, frank, mild, and amiable; it resembles the inward life itself, from which these properties are derived into the outward man.

It concludes by introducing the gentler, air-like qualities of the sanguine temperament.</summary>

40. If the soul is surrounded by this temperament <note>The Sanguine complexion, associated with the element of Air.</note>, and sets its imagination into it and chooses to live according to it, then it shows itself to be friendly, subtle, and eager to search and dive into many things for which it has an open door. This is because the soul receives and experiences within this temperament all that the constellation <note>The astrological alignment or planetary influence.</note> or the influence of the stars forms. It is naturally cheerful, yet soon frightened and confused by the terrors of the "fire-power" <note>An intense, sudden surge of anger or spiritual heat.</note>; however, it remains resolute within itself, firm in its own thoughts and opinions, and does not seek the advice or judgment of others. Through this temperament, it possesses a sharp understanding regarding outward matters. Furthermore, it is not inclined to do mischief when angry; though its spirit is easily raised to a height, it subsides again just as quickly, exactly like the fluctuating air does.

41. The soul that has this temperament should be exceedingly watchful, for the Devil is enraged against it, being unable to gain much ground within this specific temperament. Therefore, he endeavors to perplex the soul with a variety of imaginations so that it might not fix its mind and thoughts upon the Kingdom of God. He presents various things before it in order to occupy its time and attention, and the soul accordingly distracts <note>original: "amuses"; in this context, it means to keep the mind occupied or lead it astray with diversions.</note> itself with various studies and pursuits. For the stars cast or inject their influence into the air, from which the fancy or imaginative faculty—which is strong and powerful in this temperament—gathers many strange, wild, and wandering ideas.

42. Such a person leads an easy, sociable, friendly, and peaceable life with everyone, yet the Devil violently stirs up his enemies against him. Because of this, he suffers much, but he passes through it easily, just as the soft air glides through all things; consequently, he is seldom very sorrowful or dejected.

43. Since the fiery temperament has no place in his heart, terror does not burn so fiercely within him. But he should particularly beware of unchastity and idolatry (or fixing his imagination and affections on any created person or thing), for through these avenues the Devil gains access even into this temperament.

## III. *Of the* PHLEGMATIC COMPLEXION.

44. *The Phlegmatic temperament* <note>original: "Phlegmatick Complexion"</note> corresponds to the element of Water. If the soul is clothed with this temperament and feeds its life's principle with it, then it displays a dull, heavy, rough, and stubborn <note>original: "perverse"</note> set of manners and conversation. It naturally dwells in a heavy body and has a poor understanding; yet, through diligent teaching and close application, it may be brought to the knowledge of common things, provided the lunar power <note>The astrological influence of the Moon, associated with water and instability.</note> does not interfere. For then the person is a mere clod of heavy earth; yet, through that same influence of the moon, he often becomes inclined toward wickedness and mischief.

45. Anything may be made of this temperament. For the "water-spirit" is yielding and capable of taking on any quality <term>original: "Tincture"; a spiritual essence or characteristic stain.</term> or impression, whether it be good or bad. This temperament also makes a hypocritical show of holiness and claims for itself the character of a righteous and upright life, but with a very great mixture of the opposite—in which it resembles the yielding and reflective quality of water.

46. The soul in this temperament is also not easily drawn into God's anger or the "dark world" <note>The realm of spiritual darkness or hellish influence.</note> which lies hidden at its center; instead, it gives in more freely and readily to the abominations of the world. It hides itself under the "water-glance" <note>A deceptive, superficial shine, like light reflecting off the surface of water.</note> or lust, supposing that to be the brightness of the Divine Light.

47. The Devil can introduce all the wickedness that he practices in Hell itself into this temperament. Indeed, if the influence of the stars does not prevent it, and the soul itself grants him admission, he gains as much advantage in this temperament as he does in the fire of the Choleric <note>The temperament associated with the element of Fire and prone to anger.</note>. For here, sin is regarded as lightly as a stream of water that passes away unnoticed.

48. **The Devil** also has power even in this <term>complexion</term><note>original: "complexion"; here referring to the Phlegmatic or "watery" temperament discussed on the previous page. In this context, a "complexion" is a person's physical and psychological constitution based on the four humors.</note> to tempt and assault the soul with sorrow and sadness when the soul gives way to him. For he darkens or obscures the radiance or luster of the "water" with the foulness of sins that have entered it; he shuts up the soul in the house of darkness so that it cannot behold the light of God’s countenance. Yet if the soul is resolute and valiant in the combat, and will use force to break open the doors of its prison of sadness, he cannot stand his ground here for long. The temperament is too weak; he can hold out better in the "fire" <note>Referring to the Choleric temperament, which is characterized by the element of fire.</note>.

### IV. Of the MELANCHOLY TEMPERAMENT.

49. **The** *Melancholy temperament* resembles the sad earth, whose properties it shares. This temperament always stands in fear before the fierce wrath of God, which entered the earth at the Creation. Within this temperament, one can find a considerable understanding along with a more than ordinary depth of thought. The chamber of this temperament stands open and is capable of great knowledge, provided that sorrow or perplexity do not stand in its way.

50. If the soul is enclosed and absorbed by this temperament—taking its nourishment and vital strength from it—then its fire burns very darkly. It drags on a life of sadness and makes little account of any worldly pomp or pleasure; however, because of the temperament, it is in perpetual heaviness and anxiety. The Devil assaults it sorely and would gladly thrust it headlong into the full depth of his darkness. For where darkness predominates, he can and does freely enter.

51. He places strange representations and frightful images before the soul, terrifying it with his intrusive suggestions and with horrid thoughts, so that it might despair of God’s grace.

52. For the soul in this chamber of *Melancholy* does not naturally admit anything into itself from which the Devil can gain much advantage, unless the soul departs or falls away from God’s grace and becomes careless and vain. But if it does so, then indeed may this temperament help the sinner forward to become a thief, a robber, or a murderer who regards man, God, and the Devil all alike. For if the soul willfully falls away or turns aside from God’s grace and gives itself up to the power and guidance of the temperament, then that person is ready to do everything that the influence of the stars works within the temperament—with which the Devil also cooperates, mixing in his own imagination.

53. But while the soul remains in struggle against the sad temperament, there is naturally none of the four temperaments less open to sinful wickedness. For it is always in a struggle against the Devil, knowing and feeling that it has him as a very near neighbor.

54. For darkness is the Devil's proper habitation; therefore, he can and does so readily assault and tempt the melancholy soul. He wants to either keep it in the darkness or throw it down from its hope and trust in God into despair, so that it might give up the conflict. For he knows well enough what the soul can do if it kindles the light of God within itself; he knows it can utterly burn up and destroy his strongest hold. If the soul succeeds, the Devil would stand in great shame, and his crafty wiles would be made manifest and exposed.

55. If the soul is once enlightened with the light of God, there is no temperament in which the Devil's will and suggestions may be more clearly discovered than in the Melancholy. This is well known by those who have been tempted and have resolutely and successfully stormed his fort. In this temperament of their nature, once enlightened, they immediately see what a foul, shameless bird <note>A metaphorical description of the Devil as a predatory or unclean scavenger.</note> he is. After such a defeat, he is not quickly eager to come near the soul again, unless he finds it on his own ground—that is, secure and negligent, and returning into the "house of sin." Then, indeed, he comes.

fawning upon it like a dog, so that it might not know him. He strews sugar upon its food, making it believe all it does to be right and good, until he can bring it again into the <term>complexion</term> <note>In Early Modern medicine, "complexion" refers to a person's temperament or humor (sanguine, phlegmatic, choleric, or melancholy)</note>, to eat the food of sorrow there.

56. Oh, how subtly and maliciously does the devil spread his nets for the unwary soul, as a fowler <note>a hunter of birds</note> does for birds! Oftentimes he terrifies it in its prayers, especially in the night when it is dark, injecting his suggestions into it and filling it with fearful apprehensions that the wrath of God is ready to seize and destroy it. Thus he makes a show as if he had power over the soul of man and as if it were his property, whereas he has not power to touch a hair of its head. Unless the soul itself despairs, and by that means gives itself up to him, he dares not spiritually and really seize or even touch it. Only through the imagination, indeed, by way of the <term>complexion</term>, can he slip or thrust his temptations into it.

57. And indeed, the reason why he so tempts and assaults the melancholy soul is that its "complexion-chamber" is dark. For he cannot insinuate his <term>imagination</term> <note>here meaning his mental images or influences</note> into the light, which is more predominant in the other three complexions. So he cannot do it there, except by or through man's own sin. But into this [melancholy] complexion he can readily and easily introduce his influence, as it is of a nature or quality so near and congenial to his own. For the dark desire of this complexion produces darkness, which contains fear or terror because of the property of the "crude rough earth" so predominant within it. Were it not for this, he would have no more right or power in this than in the other complexions. As it is, he can achieve no more within the imagination than to terrify a man and make him sad and fearful.

58. But the devil has more than one kind of temptation for the melancholy soul. For, if he cannot persuade it to absolutely despair of God's mercy and so give itself up to him that way, he brings it—when over-burdened with fears and sad apprehensions about its present state and future doom, and impatient under the weight of them—to thoughts and designs of self-murder <note>original: Self-Murther; suicide</note>. For he dares not destroy a man; the man himself must do that, for the soul has free will. If it resists the devil and will not do as he counsels it, then, however he may tempt, he still does not have the power to touch even the outward and sinful body. He boasts of such power, but he is a liar. If he had it, he would soon show it.

59. But it is not so. Christ has, by entering into death and the dark dungeon of hell, opened the gates of heaven to all souls; every person may now freely enter in. The devil's chain, with which he bound and tied the soul in Adam <note>a reference to the "Fall of Man" and original sin</note>, was broken on the Cross. Oh, how unwilling is that grand enemy of souls to hear of the Cross! Which, if seriously and earnestly applied in the work of both faith and <term>mortification</term> <note>the spiritual practice of subduing one's worldly desires and sins</note>, is deadly poison to him.

60. The devil is always objecting to the melancholy man about the heinousness of his guilt, and how impossible it is for him to obtain God's pardon and grace; and he then prompts him to despair and, consequently, to stab, drown, or hang himself, or in any other way put an end to his miserable life, so that he (the devil) may thereby gain access or entrance into the deluded victim's soul. For otherwise, he neither dares nor can touch it.

61. But if he can prevail upon it to actually and fully consent to his suggestions, so as to resolve to put them into practice, then he is like the executioner who binds the prisoner and brings him forth to death. Yet even then, he dares to execute nothing upon it until the soul has put itself into his power through such an act of suicide.

<summary>This page explains that while the devil targets the "melancholy" temperament due to its natural darkness, he has no actual power over the soul unless the individual chooses to despair or commit suicide. It emphasizes that Christ's sacrifice broke the devil's legal claim over humanity, leaving the soul with the free will to resist temptation.</summary>

# The Third Chapter.

## Showing how to deal with the Prince of Darkness, when he tempts the Poor Soul to Despair.

---

62. <image-desc>Decorative initial letter T featuring intricate floral and foliage scrollwork.</image-desc> THE Devil is a stubborn, proud, and haughty spirit; and a person cannot repel him more effectively than by resisting him with a cheerful, bold, and courageous heart, without showing the least fear of him; for he has no more power than a piece of straw. Simply despise him; reproach him with the shame and depth of his fall; tell him how, from such a fair and glorious angel, he has now become a black devil.

63. *When he first comes, do not argue with him at all; when he presents to you the register or catalogue of your sins, and pleads his power over and right of access to you because of them, give him no answer on that point. But when he assaults your soul by injecting into its imagination evil thoughts of God, along with the horror of your past sins, and acts as if he would snatch you away in a sudden and terrible flash of lightning—then bear up with fresh courage against him and say, "Where do you come from, you black wretch? I thought you had been in Heaven among the angels; how is it that you have been expelled from there and loaded with the record of God’s anger? I thought you had been a prince in God’s presence; how then have you become his executioner? Has so fair an angel become a lowly executioner? <note>original: "base Executioner"</note> Shame on you; what do you have to do here with me? Go away to the angels in Heaven if you are God’s servant. Shame on you, get out of here, you servile executioner of God’s wrath: go to your own angels; you have nothing to do here." This potion <note>In this context, a "potion" refers to a spiritual remedy or a verbal rebuttal intended to drive away the Devil.</note>, I trust, he will readily swallow; it is for his health.*

64. But if he will not flinch for this, but continues to read to you the register or catalogue of your sins, then stand boldly before him and say, *"Listen! Read this in answer to that charge: The offspring <note>original: "Seed"</note> of the woman shall bruise or crush the serpent’s head. <note>A reference to Genesis 3:15, traditionally interpreted as a prophecy of Christ's victory over the Devil.</note> Can you not find it? Wait a little, I will light a candle to help you. It stands recorded in the beginning of the Bible, in the same place as Adam’s fall. For the woman’s offspring shall crush or bruise your head."* This is the second potion for him to take.

65. Perhaps he will not yet retreat, but will go on to argue that you are a great sinner and have willfully and purposely committed this or that great sin, well knowing that it was wrong; and that you were trying to cover your filthiness all the while with the fair mantle of God’s grace, while the principle of God’s anger was actually ignited in you at the same time—and that you are therefore now the Devil’s own property.

66. Thus, through the suggestions <note>original: "Injections"</note> from the Devil’s imagination, the poor soul is many times terrified and brought to think itself such a terrible <note>original: "heinous"</note> sinner that God has forsaken it because of its sins, and that the Devil will carry it away and cast it into the pit of Hell! This dreadful apprehension makes the soul exceedingly afraid of him.

67. But now, when he comes in such a frightening disguise, take heart once more through the Spirit of Christ and say, *"I still have a medicine for you, Satan, that might—if you can use it—help you return to your former angelic state. Here, take this, and say to yourself if you can: The blood of Jesus Christ cleanses us from all our sins; and again, The Son of Man has come to seek and to save that which was lost."*

68. *"What would you give, Devil, for this precious remedy—that God had become man, or incarnate, in you? I always have an open door of grace into that blessed redemption, but—"*

# A Treatise of the Four Complexions. Chap. 3.

...you have not. You are only a liar; go away from here, you have nothing in me. Although it is true that I am a sinner, the guilt is chiefly yours. You, through your deceit and treachery, worked the sin in me. Take back then what is yours—the sin. The sufferings and death of Jesus Christ are mine. He became man for the purpose of delivering us from the guilt and power of sin. You have produced the sin in me; keep that for yourself. My Lord Jesus Christ has produced in me, in my nature, the righteousness which is valid before God; that, I keep for myself. His sufferings and his dying for sin are mine. He has died for the sin I have committed and has risen again in his righteousness; he has included my soul in his satisfaction <note>The theological concept that Christ's sacrifice "satisfied" the debt of sin owed to God's justice.</note>. Christ is in me, and I am in him; and my sin is in you, and you are in hell.

69. Mock him even further, and say: "Fair angel, you who would not stay even one day in heaven: you were a high-ranking official <note>original: "Hierarch"</note> there, and now you boast about your list of the filthy sins of men. You vile executioner, take away my sins in your beggarly bag <note>original: "Wallet"</note>; you are only a receiver and bearer of sins. Carry them to the anger of God, which is your lord and master. In this way, I shall be rid of them, and only Christ's merits will remain with me."

70. *Christ said, "My sheep are in my hands, and none can take them from me; the Father who has given them to me is greater than all."*

71. O, you who were once a fair angel; how have you fallen now to become a mere bearer of a bag of sins! From a prince to a beggarly slave! Go away with your load of wickedness, and take mine along with you as well. You need nothing but the abominations of sin; you have no part in my soul. Here I stand; devour me if you can.

72. But see, I have a mark or sign in me; that is, the sign of the Cross. On that Cross, Christ slew sin and death; he destroyed hell and bound you, its prince, as a prisoner in God’s anger. Swallow this medicine <note>original: "Potion"</note> with the rest; and then perhaps you might become a fair angel again.

73. Do not let your thoughts argue with him, and do not be afraid of him. Instead, be courageous and bold, whether it is by day or by night. He dares to do you no harm, even if you insult him in the most taunting and bitter manner imaginable, provided he gives you a reason to do so. Otherwise, do not insult him.

74. If the sadness or fear of the soul is not accompanied by a degree of outward fright and dismay, then the Devil is not actually there. Instead, it is only the soul's own terror at the inward stirrings and motions that arise from the dark abyss—the awakened principle of God’s wrath within itself. Often, when the melancholy disposition <note>original: "Complexion"; in this context, the "humor" of black bile associated with sadness and introspection.</note> is stirred up by the fierce and wrathful influence of the stars, the soul thinks that the Devil is present, when that is not the case at all.

75. When he does come, he comes either dressed in his own natural display of terror, in the guise of an angel of light, or rather in the fawning way of a dog.

76. If he comes to you in the dark, and for that reason frightens you all the more, do not leave the place for him and do not run away; he is not so important that a person should give way to him.

77. Mock and scorn him even in the darkness, and say, *"Are you there? I thought you were an angel of light, and yet do you stand there, leering in the dark like a thief? If it is the filth and stench of sin that you are looking for, there are many places fouler and better suited for you than this."* If he comes to you as himself, in his natural form or clothing of terror, receive him in this manner. Otherwise, do not give him any reason to approach you through unprovoked insults.

79. He does not easily terrify a courageous man who does not flinch from him, especially if that man opposes and scorns him. For the Devil is still a proud spirit and always wants to be the master of whatever place he is in. If a man will not give way or leave him, the Devil is foiled and disappointed, and will not stay there long. But if he goes away leaving a stench, then leave the place instantly, and say, "Shame on you, you foul coward <note>original: "Caitiff"</note>, how..."

# Chap. 3. A Treatise of the Four Complexions.

"How strongly you smell of your dungeon!" Repulsed in this way, he will not return in a hurry with his boasting.

79. Do not let your mind engage in any kind of dispute with him; he is not worth that much attention. Print only this one simple text or saying on your memory: *The blood of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, cleanses us from all our sins.* You have enough argument here, and you need no other comfort.

80. Wrap all your thoughts in that; let no other thought come from your heart. Let the Devil suggest to you, or insinuate into your imagination, whatever he wants; believe everything he says to be a lie, but believe that saying or text to be a fixed and certain truth. Hold fast to that as your own, despite all his sly whispers and suggestions to the contrary.

81. Do not seek out many arguments or texts of Scripture against his terrifying assaults; he is too crafty for you in that matter. For he tears the first and best ones out of your heart, so that you might forget them or doubt them. Wrap your soul only in that one text; it is strong enough to withstand him. If you wrap your soul in it, you can easily put him to shame; he cannot touch you, nor will he stay long with you. If you do not give in to him, then he becomes a scoff and a laughingstock to the demons employed as his agents among mankind, as well as to the holy angels. But in general, he will not keep his ground long enough to endure all this insult and scorn. So, if you manfully resist him in this way, *he will flee from you*, as the Scripture says.

82. Often repeat that one saying or text; fix it and lay it up in your heart, and strengthen your courage against him from it. The Spirit which lies hidden in that holy text will assist you well enough. Though your soul trembles before him, resist him even in that fierce wrath, which is his own principle. <note>The author suggests using the intensity of faith to counteract the "fierce wrath" or dark nature of the Devil.</note> You may venture your life upon it; nothing will hurt you. He dares use no force, nor indeed does he have any. He neither dares, nor is he able, to do any hurt to the soul during its life in the body.

83. For Christ has opened the Door of Grace, which accordingly now stands open in and to the soul of every poor sinner while he lives upon the earth. Christ did, in his own soul, break open that iron gate which was shut fast in the soul of man because of God’s anger awakened within it.

84. Now all souls have a communion or sympathy with that one soul of Jesus Christ. They all come from one original root and are all together like one tree with many branches. Therefore, his breaking open that enclosure, and the grace or benefit obtained by it, is passed from him into and upon all souls, from *Adam* to the last man that shall exist. The Door of Grace stands open in and to them all. God himself has barred it to no one; nor is it indeed shut to any except those who voluntarily exclude themselves. The mark or sign of his entrance into humanity—of taking the human nature upon himself—is manifested in and to all souls. And therefore, the neglect and contempt of it will be a charge and evidence against the ungodly at the Day of Judgment.

85. Though our sins, as *Isaiah* says, *were as scarlet*, yet the Door of Grace and mercy stands open to every sinner, for in his conversion *they shall become white as snow*. The same prophet *Isaiah* also says, *Can a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? Yes, they may forget, yet I will not forget you: For behold, I have engraved or signed you upon the palms of my hands*; that is, in his hands pierced through with nails, and in the wound of his side, he has marked or signed the "soul of all souls." <note>This implies that Christ's suffering represents and encompasses the suffering and redemption of all humanity.</note>

86. Now if anyone will not come and lay himself therein, but instead chooses to despise the print or mark of Christ’s wounds, or allows the Devil to cover and hide it from him,

He is himself at fault. But, though the Devil covers it, yet it still remains engraved or imprinted in the greatest sinner that is in the world. For *Isaiah* says in the Spirit of Christ:
> *Though a mother should forget her child, which she can very hardly do, yet he will not forget his love and grace, promised, yes, given to man.*

87. He has not forgotten any soul, even if it were blood-red with sin: For he has engraved or imprinted it in his blood and death; not some souls only, but the whole tree of the human soul, with its root and branches. *As sin came from one upon all; so also came the righteousness through Christ upon all. As sin passed from one upon all to death; so also the righteousness out of Christ passed from one upon all to life,* says the Apostle <note>Referring to the Apostle Paul in Romans 5:18.</note>.

88. But the fact that all men do not partake of this benefit is through their own fault. Their will is free; and God wills that all men should be saved. The Psalmist also says, *You are not a God that wills evil:* To which may be added God's own declaration of himself by his prophet Ezekiel: *As I live, says the Lord; I do not desire the death of a sinner; but that he convert and live.*

89. Therefore no soul should think or say within itself, *the measure of my sin is full; God has forsaken or rejected me; I cannot be saved.* Oh NO. He has imprinted you in his hands, in the wounds, marks, or prints of the nails. You are a branch growing on the great tree of all souls, and have sympathy and communion with it, as a branch has with the tree. All the time that you live in this world, even so long as you are clothed with flesh and blood, you stand in that tree, and partake of the redeemed nature and virtue of it.

# The Fourth Chapter.

## Of the Temptation arising from the Complexion and Influence of the Stars.

90. All temptation does not come from the Devil, especially that which attacks melancholy men, most of whose sorrow or sadness proceeds from the imagination of the soul. Since the soul is forced to take up its abode in a <term>melancholy</term> <note>original: "melancholy Inn"; here meaning the physical body dominated by the "black bile" or melancholy temperament.</note> inn or lodging, it is easily made sad and heavy by it; and is brought to think that God has forgotten or forsaken it, and will not accept it.

91. For the *melancholy <term>complexion</term>* <note>original: "complexion"; in early modern medicine, this refers to the specific balance of "humors" (fluids) that determines a person's physical and mental temperament.</note> is naturally dark. It has no light of its own, as the other complexions have. Yet this darkness of temperament is not of the essence or substance of the soul; it is only the soul’s dwelling-house, during its sojourning in the earthly body.

92. Therefore the soul’s holiness or righteousness is not at all founded on the complexion, nor depends upon it, but has its root and ground in heaven, or in the inward heavenly <term>Principle</term> <note>Boehme uses "Principles" to describe different realms of existence; the Second Principle is the divine world of light and love.</note> wherein God dwells: According to the words of St. *Paul* to the *Philippians*; *Our conversation is in heaven.* <note>original: "Conversation"; in the 17th century, this meant "citizenship" or "way of life."</note> This *heaven*, where God dwells, is not manifested in the physical temperament, but only in itself, in the Second Principle.

93. It often happens that the most holy souls are thus afflicted and overwhelmed with sorrow. God indeed permits it to be so, to the end that they may be tested; and wrestle the more earnestly for the triumphal crown or noble garland of victory.

94. The Crown of Triumph—with which the soul is rewarded and adorned after having taken Heaven, as it were, by storm through great constancy and perseverance in the conflicts of this life—is much more noble, bright, and glorious than the crown that is not obtained until after the death of the body, when it is first placed upon the soul.

95. For the Revelation of Jesus Christ says: 
> *Whoever overcomes, to him I will give the right to sit with me upon my throne, just as I have overcome and am set down with my Father upon his throne. Also, whoever overcomes, to him will I give to eat of the hidden manna; and I will give him a good testimony; and with that testimony a new name written, which no one knows except he who has received it.*

96. But to return to the natural cause of sadness in the melancholic temperament <note>original: "melancholy Complexion"</note>. There often occurs a malignant conjunction of the stars, or an eclipse of the sun and moon. If this conjunction or alignment falls within an earthly zodiac sign, and Mars casts his poisonous rays or baleful influence into it, then the influence of this evil conjunction greatly disturbs and terrifies a soul that is involved or immersed in the melancholic temperament. Because of this, the soul is kept in continual apprehension that the fierce anger of God, or the Devil, is at hand and ready to devour it.

97. For when the soul feels the venomous rays of Mars within its temperament, and finds itself placed in a dark "inn" or lodging <note>The "inn" refers to the physical body or the current state of the soul's temperament.</note>, it begins to fear that God has rejected or reprobated <term>reprobated: excluded from salvation; damned</term> it, and will not accept it. This is especially true when the soul imagines or broods so deeply into its temperament that it "eats" of the poison of Mars and ignites its fire-life <note>fire-life: A term used by Boehme to describe the soul’s essential spiritual energy or drive.</note> with it. Then, indeed, there arises within it a most bitter anxiety and a fear of both the Devil and God's anger.

98. Then the soul begins to speculate and think that God has not predestined or elected it in Christ to eternal life. It becomes so dejected that it dares not lift up its face to God, but cries out continually that it is one of the greatest of sinners and that the door of grace is shut against it. Yet all of this is actually nothing more than a fantasy <note>original: "Phantasy"; here meaning a mental delusion or false perception</note> arising from the temperament when it is disturbed by a malign influence of the stars, which thus vexes or torments the soul.

99. For when the spirit of the great world <note>original: "Spirit of the Great World," referring to the macrocosm or the universal spirit of the physical universe</note> has, through the constellation or power of the stars, insinuated itself into the temperament, it plays its "juggling tricks" there and introduces strange fancies into the imagination. Consequently, the soul inwardly afflicts or torments itself, and the outward spirit also eventually becomes totally inflamed in its earthly source or quality. From this, it happens that the "Wheel," or third form in the center of nature <note>A reference to Boehme's mystical description of the mechanics of the soul and nature.</note>, is set spinning so violently that the spirit cannot take hold of or steady its hurried thoughts and senses. This inflamed agitation of the mind is what properly constitutes frenzy or madness, and it often seizes people of a melancholic temperament.

100. Now, when the Devil sees that effect wrought, he weaves his own imagination into it, and thereby agitates and torments the soul even more. But he has no actual authority or power over the soul; it is only that the source or principle of anxiety in the soul is the very same source or quality as his own life. Therefore, he is a ready and present guest in such a "lodging." For, except in this specific source or principle, he stands in total opposition to human nature.

101. Therefore, let no one who is thus tormented with the temptation of sadness arising from their temperament imagine that their anguish and trouble of mind proceed from any principle of anger or lack of mercy in God. For it is nothing other than a fantasy caused in the imagination by the temperament of one's nature and the influence of the stars upon it.

102. For we see daily that the most foul and "fat swine" of the Devil's herd—those who wallow every day and hour in sin—are not tempted and troubled in this way. The reason is that they have an outward light in their temperament, in which they "dance" after the Devil, appear—

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "melancholy" temperament (associated with sadness and spiritual anxiety), arguing that feelings of abandonment are not evidence of God’s rejection, but rather a sign of His presence.</meta>

<page-num>142</page-num>
# A Treatise of the Four Complexions. Chapter 4.

...appearing to them in the form of an angel. But as long as there is the least spark of divine light glimmering in any person who desires the grace of God and wishes to partake of His salvation, God’s door of grace remains open to them.

103. For he who is truly forsaken or rejected by God—one whose measure of sin is full—regards neither God, man, nor the Devil. Instead, he is completely blind and continues in a course of carelessness, vanity, and wickedness without fear. He follows a customary routine of formal worship and finds satisfaction in it. Like a beast going into a church and a beast coming out again, he has no <term>experimental knowledge</term> <note>original: "experimental Knowledge" – knowledge gained through personal, lived experience rather than just theory or hearsay</note> of God. All his religion is mere imagination, opinion, fiction, and habit, yet he looks upon this and trusts it as his sanctification.

104. From this, the <term>melancholy mind</term> <note>original: "melancholy Mind" – a person suffering from the "melancholy" temperament, which in this era was believed to cause deep depression, anxiety, and spiritual fear</note> may perceive that God does not fully manifest His anger in this life. For although the ungodly are indeed punished in this life, they do not recognize their punishments as being inflicted by the hand of God; instead, they see them as misfortunes happening by chance and accident.

105. But that the trouble of mind discussed here is a subject of God’s pity rather than His wrath is sufficiently proven by the Prophet *Isaiah*. Treating the person and spirit of Christ, he says, *He will not break the bruised reed, nor extinguish the smoking flax* <note>original: "bruised Reed... smoking Flax" – metaphors for a person who is spiritually fragile or whose faith is a barely glowing ember</note>. A comforting proof of this same truth is also seen in the blessed call and promise of *Jesus Christ* Himself in *St. Matthew’s Gospel*: *Come to me, all you who are weary and heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am meek and lowly in heart, and you shall find rest for your souls.*

Now, the "yoke" or "cross" of Christ is nothing other than the cross of nature and providence. That is to say, it is whatever happens to a person, whether in the ordinary course of nature or by the special order of providence—whether it be inward or outward temptation, persecution, cares, troubles, necessities, sickness, pain, and affliction of either body or mind. This is the yoke or cross which a person is required to *take up and carry after Christ* with patience, committing themselves to the love and mercy of God with full resignation. When this is done, the affliction—whatever it may be—is so far from hurting the soul that it actually does much good.

106. For while the soul stays in the "House of Sorrow," it is not in the "House of Sin," nor in the pride, pomp, and pleasure of the world. God holds the soul back with tribulation, as if with a fatherly restraint, from the sinful pleasures of this world. And if one must be in trouble and sorrow for a little while, alas, what does it matter? How soon will the soul be released from its mournful prison and receive the triumphal crown of everlasting joy?

107. O Eternity, you are very long! What is it for a soul to be in affliction for a moment, only to afterwards receive an exceeding and eternal weight of glory? For God will *wipe away all tears from the eyes of his redeemed people.* As long as there is a single spark of good desire in the soul that pants or longs after God’s Spirit, God’s Spirit is present within that little spark.

108. For a person’s breathing and longing after God does not come from the current corrupted nature of man himself; rather, it is the "drawing" of the Father, through His Son *Jesus Christ*, to Himself. The Holy Spirit is itself the Divine Desire. No one can desire God without His Spirit, which exists within that desire and keeps the will of the desire steadfast in God. By this, the poor soul is preserved from falling away.

109. *St. Paul* says, *We do not know what we should say before God when we pray; but the Spirit of God helps us mightily with sighs and groans that cannot be uttered, according to what pleases God.* Why then should we doubt His grace and goodwill toward us any longer, when He is always more willing and ready to receive us into His mercy than we are to go to Him?

## Chap. 4.

110. Just observe what the Father did for the lost son, who had wasted the inheritance or portion he had received from him on the Devil's "fattened swine" <note>original: "fatted Swine"; a reference to the Prodigal Son's degradation and base sins</note>, and had become a naked, filthy swineherd. As soon as the Father saw the Prodigal returning to him, he fell upon his neck and kissed him, saying, *This my dearly beloved son, whom I had lost, has come home again; he was dead, and has become living.* He then commanded all his household to make a feast and to rejoice with him for the recovery of his lost son. Christ himself presents this parable to us as a true and comfortable representation of the divine mercy and pardon ready for penitent sinners; he tells us *that there is more joy in the Kingdom of Heaven among the angels of God for one sinner that repents, than for ninety-nine just persons who need no repentance.*

111. Now, the lost Prodigal Son is none other than the poor sinful human being, when he becomes aware of how great a sinner he has been and intends to seek God's mercy. Then does our dear and loving Father in Christ run to meet him and receive him with great joy. The angels and the blessed souls in heaven also rejoice exceedingly that a precious soul of a dear brother has come to them out of the house of sin and death.

112. The troubled soul is prone to perplex and torment itself because it cannot, through its own desire, open the spring of divine joy in the heart. It sighs, laments, and fears that God will have nothing to do with it because it cannot feel the comfort of his noticeable presence. It also looks at other people who are fellow travelers in the same Christian pilgrimage and sees them cheerful and merry. From this, it mistakenly assumes that their cheerfulness comes solely from a divine principle of love and joy in their souls; it concludes that it is not accepted or chosen, but rather rejected by God. It desperately wants to feel the comfortable presence of God in the heart.

113. Before the time of my *illumination* <note>The author’s personal mystical awakening or spiritual breakthrough</note> and *high knowledge*, it was just the same with me. I went through a long and sore conflict before I obtained my noble garland <term>noble garland: a metaphor for spiritual victory or the crown of life</term>; and only then did I first learn how God does not dwell in the outward, fleshly heart, but in the center of the soul in himself—that is, in his own principle.

114. Then I also first perceived in my interior or inward spirit that it was God himself who had thus drawn me to him in and through my desire. I did not understand this before; I thought the good desire was my own, and that God was far distant from us humans. But afterward, I clearly found—and rejoiced to find—how God is so gracious to us. Therefore, I write this as an example and caution to others, telling them not to give way to despair when the Comforter <note>The Holy Spirit</note> delays his coming. Instead, think of that consoling encouragement left to us in David's Psalm: *Heaviness may endure for a night, but joy comes in the morning.*

115. It has been no different for the greatest saints of God. They were forced to wrestle long and earnestly for the noble garland. Indeed, no one will be crowned with it unless they wrestle, strive for it, and overcome in the conflict.

116. It is indeed deposited or laid up in the soul, but in the <term>Second Principle</term> <note>In the author's (Jacob Boehme's) theology, the Second Principle is the realm of Light and Love, while the First Principle is the dark, fiery origin of nature</note>; whereas the soul itself, as to its essence and life, stands fixed in the First Principle. Therefore, if the soul wishes to put on 그 crown during this mortal life, it must wrestle for it. And even if it does not obtain it in this world, it will certainly receive it after it has put off this <term>earthly tabernacle</term> <note>The physical body</note>. For Christ says, *In the world you shall have anxiety and trouble, but in me, peace. And, be of good comfort, I have overcome the world.*

117. The noble and precious pearl <note>A metaphor for spiritual truth or the presence of Christ</note> lies in many a tempted and troubled mind, much closer to being born and manifested than it is in some who suppose themselves to be in full possession and enjoyment of it. But it withdraws and hides itself in the darkness of such souls and refuses to shine forth. But let that not frighten or trouble any—

one. For where it is in the fullest reality and measure, there it will make the least show of itself.

118. It hides itself for this reason: so that the soul, in its intense hunger and anxious desire for it, should seek it with even greater earnestness, and by that means share more fully in its refreshing spirit and regenerating virtue. For Christ says, *Seek, and then you shall find; knock, and then it will be opened unto you*; and in another place, *My Father will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him for it*. Lay hold of this promise of God with a most assured faith and firm confidence; and even though your misgiving heart says "no" to it, do not be persuaded to let go of your hold.

119. For to believe is not simply to be filled with joy in the physical heart and outward <term>complexion</term> <note>original: "complexion"; the dominant temperament or physical and mental makeup of a person</note>, or for the mind and animal spirits <term>animal spirits</term> <note>In the 17th century, these were thought to be subtle fluids that acted as the bridge between the soul and the body's movements.</note> to be so elevated that the heart and kidneys leap for joy. This is not true faith, but only glimpses of love or emanations from the Holy Spirit—a transient glimpse or sudden flash of the heavenly life that is not steady or permanent.

120. For God does not dwell in the outward heart or temperament, but in himself—in the second principle <note>original: "second Centre or Principle"; in Boehme’s mystical theology, this refers to the divine world of light and love.</note>, in the "jewel" of the soul, that noble image or likeness of God which is hidden from this outward world.

121. But true faith is when the spirit of the soul, with its will and desire, enters into and thirsts for that which it neither sees nor feels.

122. *Observe*: The soul, in its own essence, does not exist in time or the physical world; yet it sends the subtle "will-spirit," which originates out of its fire-life <note>Boehme describes the soul's fundamental energy as a "fire-life" that must be transformed by divine light.</note>, into the world. In that very will-spirit, the pearl <note>A metaphor for the "Pearl of Great Price," representing the spark of Christ or divine light within the soul.</note> is conceived; and then the soul's "fire" no longer remains in earthly desire.

123. For as long as the pearl remains in the will-spirit, the good desire remains in the soul. For that little pearl is a spark of divine love; it is the Father drawing the soul into his love.

124. The soul, therefore, should stand firm in its desire toward God, even though human reason—arising from the dark temperament—flatly opposes it and denies that God is present within. For if God were not present in the soul, it could have no will or desire for him. Where God is not present in the spirit of the will, the soul is, as it were, completely blind and dead to God. It feels no need or desire for God at all, nor any wish to share in his nature, but lives and plays in the "heaven" of its own outward light and rational powers. In this condition, it only has a more subtle skill and faculty of understanding than the animals, because its natural essence has a higher origin than theirs.

125. An anxious mind, therefore, should by no means allow its temperament to betray it into believing that God is not present or is unwilling to receive it. For when the soul feeds on such a hopeless conclusion, it becomes exceedingly overwhelmed with anguish.

126. It is indeed a great sin for the mind to dwell on a fantasy so vain and reproachful to God. For the soul, which is a noble creature born out of God's nature, is cast into great and unnecessary anxiety by it. This imagination kindles the soul's fire, so that it burns in the "painful source" <note>original: "painful Source or Principle"; Boehme’s term for the soul's state of raw, agonizing hunger when separated from God's light.</note>.

127. *Dear soul*, think of it this way when the painful quality of your temperament is stirred up by the influence of the stars <note>original: "Constellation"; early modern medicine and theology often linked planetary movements to human moods and health.</note> working within it: realize that it proceeds from that cause alone, and from nothing else. Consider at the same time that you then stand as a worker in God's vineyard, where you should labor and not stand idle, for you do God great service by doing so. Your appointed task is to overcome the temptation that assaults you through a firm faith, even if no comfort arises in your outward heart to encourage and support you in the struggle.

128. But so that you may not be discouraged or deceived in this important matter, observe and remember that true faith does not consist in believing what you see or feel. Instead, true faith is to trust the hidden Spirit and believe its Word against reason, sense, and nature—and to do so so immovably that you would rather let go of your body’s life than your trust and hold on its promise. This is the faith which wrestles powerfully with God, as *Jacob* did all night <note>Refers to Genesis 32:24–30, where Jacob wrestles with a divine figure.</note>. It is a faith which neither sees nor feels anything, and yet trusts or relies upon the promised Word. This is the faith which overcomes God, as *Jacob's* did when it was said to him: *You have wrestled with God and man, and have prevailed.*

129. If you ask what Word or promise I mean, I answer: it is this. *My Father will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him for it.* That is the same Holy Spirit of which Christ himself also spoke, saying: *When he comes, he will lead you into all truth; for he will receive from me, and make it known to you.*

130. But so that you may harbor no doubt that this temptation, terror, and dejection proceed entirely from the influence and effect of the <term>Complexion</term> <note>original: "Complexion"; here meaning one's biological temperament or "humor" (Melancholic, Choleric, Sanguine, or Phlegmatic) which was believed to dictate personality and health.</note> upon the soul, I will set an example or case before you. This may happen even to a choleric (fiery) temperament, and much more so to a melancholy (earthly) one.

131. If you walk alone in any dark or dismal place at night, you are apt to be afraid, thinking that there is something in the dark that may frighten you. Now, what kind of fear is this, and where does it come from? Is the flesh afraid of danger to itself? No; for if it were, it would not go there at all. Rather, it is the poor confined soul, which is a prisoner in the flesh and in the complexion, that is afraid in the darkness. It always has a dread that the devil may lay hold of it, for it knows that he dwells in the darkness; therefore, it is afraid he will try to catch it. From this circumstance and consideration, it is plain enough that the fear comes from the <term>fantasy</term> <note>original: "Phantasy"; the imaginative faculty of the mind.</note> or imagination of the soul while it is staying in the strange lodging of the complexion.

132. This is how it goes with the poor soul that is walled up in the gloomy chamber of *Melancholy*. It is in such perpetual terror and dejection that its thoughts cannot lift themselves up, but instead grovel and grope around in the dark, standing in continual fear of the devil and the anger of God.
