<header>Of the worthy Preparation to the Holy Testament. Ch. 4.</header>

## Of the worthy Preparation to the Holy Testament of Christ.

19. **IF** anyone calls himself a Christian, and comforts himself with the merits of **Christ**, and approaches his **Testament** <term>The "Holy Testament" refers here to the Eucharist or Holy Communion, reflecting the "New Testament in Christ's blood."</term> to worthily receive it, let him consider his **ways** well. Let him look to his **heart** and see how it is shaped:
1. Whether he stands in such a **desire** as to be willing to die completely to **vanity**.
2. Whether it is his **purpose** to leave all falsehood, unrighteousness, lying, and deceit, and whether he is resolved never to enter into them again.
3. Whether he desires the **grace** of God in **Christ** with a clean, *pure* **will**.
4. Also, whether he is *sorry* for his **sin**.
5. Whether he finds and feels such a will in himself that from now on he will *wholly* depart from his former sins and blasphemies.
6. Also, whether he is so minded that he will yield up his whole **heart** and **will** to God’s **mercy**.
7. Also, whether he finds, feels, and knows a **place** in himself where he will lay up this high Testament; namely, the **flesh** and **blood** of **Christ**, along with his **grace**.
8. Also, whether or not he has made **room** in his **heart** and whole **soul** for the **spirit** of **Christ**, so that he may enter there as a *living conqueror* over **death** and **hell**, and may build his royal **palace** in his **heart** and **soul**.
9. And whether he is capable of this, where **Christ** says, "*We will come to you, and make our dwelling in you*" (John 14:23).
10. Also, whether the **temple** of the **Holy Spirit** in him is swept and cleansed through true **repentance**.
11. Also, whether there is a right *mouth* in him that can rightly receive **Christ’s** holy **flesh**.
12. Also, whether the **essence** of his **life** is so shaped that **Christ**, with his **substance** and his **love**, may continue within it? For **Christ** says, "*He that eats my flesh and drinks my blood continues in me, and I in him*" (John 6:56).
13. Also, whether he finds in his **mind** that the stream of **living waters** of *divine love* flows from him—that he loves his **God**, and his brother and neighbor, as himself.
14. Also, whether he wishes and desires to do **good** to his **enemies**.
15. Whether he accounts **anything** in this world as *his own*, of which he says, "*This is mine alone*."
16. Or whether, in that which he has and possesses, he accounts himself as only a **servant** of **God** and a **steward** to him and his brother. Does he consider that he is only an **officer** and **servant** of **God** in his **state**, **condition**, and temporal **goods**—that *none* of it is his own, but **God’s** and his **brother’s**?
17. Also, whether he trusts **God** in his conduct <note>original: "Conversation"; here meaning general behavior or way of life.</note>, and keeps and esteems his **life** as his Lord **Christ** did, who was but a *traveler* in this world and had nothing of his own, and also willingly gave up his **life** for his **brethren**?
18. Also, whether he finds even a **spark** of such a **will** in himself?

20. Now, if he finds *all of this* in himself, then he is truly worthy and very fit for such **participation in the Testament**. *But if not*, yet he finds such a **hunger** in himself that he wishes he were so and desires to be so, then he is *in the drawing of the Father* <note>original: "drawing of the Father"; a reference to John 6:44: "No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him."</note> toward the **grace** in **Christ**. In that case, he should not debate long with **reason** or create **doubts** within himself. Instead, he should at that very **hour** enter into an earnest **purpose** to begin sincere **repentance**, continually flying to the **grace** of God in **Christ**. He should pray that God will give him such a **heart** and **will**, not attributing it to himself as if he could attain it by his own **power** and **virtue**. Rather, he should simply and merely sink into the most pure **grace**, into the **mercy** of God, and be like a young child who only has a **desire** for the **mother’s milk**—who cannot help himself, but flies to his **mother** so that she may help him.

21. His going to the **Communion of Saints** <term>The "Communion of Saints" refers to the spiritual fellowship of all believers and the act of joining together for the Lord's Supper.</term> should be in *humility*, with a true **reconciliation** with all those whom he has wronged or who have wronged him. He should forgive *all his enemies* and wish the same for them as he desires for himself: With

# Chapter 4: On the Worthy Preparation for the Holy Testament.

...the fear of God and a penitent heart, with a truly earnest purpose, he may approach it. He should bring no *desire of his own* to the Testament of Christ, nor should he wish to grasp or understand such grace through his own ability. Instead, he should only sink himself down and wholly give himself up to grace as one who is unworthy. He should cast himself upon that grace, letting it do with him what it will, and not desire the spirit of *divine joy* for his own sake—understand this as a personal possession—but give himself up to it and sink down into grace, so that the same Spirit of Grace may be in him *how* and *when it wills*.

**22. The heart and mind should say to itself before the Testament of God:**
> *O great Grace of God, I, an unworthy and sinful man, come to you at your call, for you have invited us poor men to come and you will refresh us (Matthew 11:28). Let it be done to me according to your word, however you will. I give myself up here wholly and completely; do with me, a poor and unworthy man, according to your grace as you will. I will be yours eternally. Break my will now, and govern it with your will; I can do nothing myself, but now I sink wholly and completely into your grace.*

23. A person who gives himself up so completely to God, and remains standing in such <term>resignation</term> <note>original: "Resignation"; in this context, it refers to 'Gelassenheit,' the spiritual practice of yielding one's personal will entirely to God</note> with his *will*, will in the end find and *feel* what grace and divine love are when grace moves within him. When the divine *fire* is kindled in his *life*, then he will feel and taste what Christ is in him, and will quickly find how he has become a different person with different thoughts and a different will.

24. And then he is a Christian: when Christ's <term>love-fire</term> <note>original: "Love-Fire"; a term used to describe the transformative, purifying power of divine love</note> struggles against God's anger in the conscience. It will be set before that person in Christ's *process* <note>original: "Process"; the spiritual journey or life-path modeled on the stages of Christ’s own life, suffering, and resurrection</note> in this world, showing that he *must follow after Christ* in his suffering, anguish, pain, scorn, and persecution. He must take the *cross* of Christ upon himself and be made conformable to *Christ's image*. Inwardly, there is a struggle against sin and the fleshly lusts within him, so that he despises himself and hates evil desires. Outwardly, he faces contempt, scorn, trouble, and misery. While the world considers him a stranger and a *fool*, and while reason views itself as foolish, he himself chooses to be a fool regarding the matters and conversations of this world, and he hates *everything* that his *flesh loves*. In this state, no one flatters him; instead, all his "good friends" shun him and withdraw, except for *a few* of the children of God who take notice and whom God sends for his comfort. Then he may realize that at that time he hangs upon the cross with Christ. He behaves in such a way that he would willingly *even die* with Christ for the sake of professing the truth, in the *hope* that he shall also arise with Christ through Christ’s *victory* and *triumph*, living eternally in Christ.

25. This is a Christian, worthy of the *Communion of Saints*, who has entered into this <term>process</term> and lives within it. All others—who attend out of habit, view Christ’s Testament as an outwardly credited *grace*, or treat it as a work done through belief alone, claiming it for themselves and receiving it as a gift without being born again or becoming a new person with new thoughts and a new will—are different. Those who keep the stained cloak of sin in their conscience and quickly return to their old ways are unworthy, unfit, and incapable of the Testament. They receive it *only to their own judgment*, as mentioned before.

<header>Of the Contention of the Learned Chap. 5.</header>

## The Fifth Chapter.

### *Of the Contention, Disputation, and Strife of the Learned about Christ's Testaments: What they effect thereby, and what is to be held concerning it.*

1. I will add this chapter not out of a desire to interfere with anyone’s good conscience, but for the comfort of the *simple children of Christ*. These people are often led into error, shut up in rigid opinions, and seduced away from true understanding by contention. Men make a mere *den of murder* out of *Christ's Testaments* <note>original: "Christ's Testaments"; here referring to the Sacraments, specifically the Lord's Supper</note> and bind the conscience in snares and chains. I wish to show these simple believers what they should think of the contentious disputations of the *learned* who rely on human reason, and what those men actually accomplish by it.

2. *Christ's Testaments* are nothing other than a *bond and covenant* between God and man; a member-like union <note>A connection like that of different parts of a single body.</note> of the children of men, where God has bound himself to man again after the Fall through the *humanity of Christ* to be their loving God. Now, all those who—*without* this member-like *bond and covenant of love*—contend and dispute about concepts and opinions regarding knowledge, are acting out of their own self-will without Christ. There is no true understanding in any such person; for *none knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal him (Matthew 11:27).*

3. Now, if Christ is revealed to and in a person, then that person has no contentious disputes or strife with anyone regarding that knowledge and skill. Instead, he is humble and considers himself unworthy of such knowledge. He despises no one because of a difference in their spiritual gifts but is in love with all people. He lets every man have his own opinion and gives his neighbor only his loving will. He considers only how he may be a *member of Christ* and a brother to his fellow believers.

<margin>* Matters.</margin>
4. But because men fall into so many opinions—and strive, contend, and dispute about them, despising one another for the *sake of the letter* <note>Following the literal text rather than the spirit.</note>, scorning others and condemning them to the Devil—the *simple Christian* should know that in all such strife there is no true understanding. It is nothing but mere pride and *Antichristian* behavior, or a miserable confusing of the words of Christ. Nothing arises from it but disunity, insecurity, and enmity; nothing else is accomplished by it but the *Devil's will*.

5. This happens because they present themselves as *teachers* of the kingdom of Christ and yet are *not sent* or recognized by God. They take their material from others and trade words and letters. They contend and dispute about the *art* <note>original: "Art"; referring to academic logic, rhetoric, or systematic theology.</note> of how men may artificially join letters together to create opinions. They argue over which composition is most "artistic" and force consciences into that human skill, but they themselves do not understand what they are doing. Their knowledge is stuck purely in the *written letters*, and they do not have the *living Word, CHRIST,* in them, who gives *testimony* to the literal word. Had they Christ’s love within them, they would share that same love and show Christ to others through themselves; they would walk in such a way that men could see they were Christ's children. But while they only contend and dispute, and will not live in love themselves, it is false—nothing but an *hypocritical show*.

6. To see that this is true, let men look at the theories about which they contend. One group of them says, *Christ is substantially present under the bread and wine.* They also say, *the bread and wine are changed into the Testament of Christ*, and there is a change of the bread and—

### Chap. 5. about Christ's Testaments. 217

<margin>Text. In the Holiness.</margin>
<margin>All-present, preferential.</margin>
...Wine; and so they will receive Christ into the animal-like and mortal man. Yet this beast-like nature is not profitable <note>original: "profitable ^b as to Holiness"</note> for **Holiness**. The second party says, "*It is only a sign and symbol of the Body of Christ, representing how he was broken or died for us*." This group denies the present, substantial partaking <note>original: "substantial Participation"</note> of Christ and understands nothing about what man is, what he lacks, or what he needs so that he may regain the salvation of God. The third party attempts to handle the matter best by sticking to the words of the institution, but they say, "*That Christ is partaken of with and under bread and wine*"; that is, *Christ's flesh and blood are eaten and drunk under bread and wine*. However, they still have no understanding of how that happens, or what part of man is capable of receiving such a gift. They refuse to know anything of the inner ground and the right <term>Adamical Humanity</term> <note>The "Adamical Humanity" refers to the original spiritual nature of humanity before the Fall, which the author believes must be restored through Christ.</note>, and they also deny the substantial inhabiting of Christ within the believer. They are as far from understanding as either of the other two groups. They do not *want* to know how this participation is achieved; they depend entirely on the dead letter of the text, while lashing out, thundering, and attacking others with insults, scorn, accusations of heresy, and blasphemy.

<margin>Imaginary.</margin>
<margin>Or, masters and dispensers.</margin>
<margin>Venerated.</margin>
7. *Every party* fights only for a literal image, wanting to bind Christ to their own **image-like opinion**. They want to be the *patron* <note>original: "Patron," meaning a defender or champion of a specific doctrine.</note> of that image, and they do this for no other reason than to achieve glory, honor, and high **esteem**. This can be seen in how they all **disgrace** and despise one another, just so each can maintain his **image-like opinion** and be called and esteemed as **lords of the mysteries of Christ**. Yet in their hearts, they respect nothing but the earthly *Lucifer* <note>In this context, "Lucifer" refers to the spirit of pride, ego, and self-will.</note>, seeking temporary honor and their own will; they wish to be **worshipped** as Christ. Every party desires it to be so—that people should worship their "image," namely, their constructed literal opinion.

8. With <term>Christ's Testaments</term> <note>The "Testaments" here refer to the Sacraments, specifically the Holy Supper or Eucharist.</note> they mark the boundaries of their images and create a sect with them, crying out, "*Here is the church of Christ; there is heresy and deception*." They say, "Cleave unto me, *here is Christ*." With this, they embitter the hearts of *kings* and *princes*, as well as the minds of the *people*, so that one brother—for the sake of an image-like opinion—despises, disgraces, slanders, and blasphemes another. He accounts him and screams at him as being devilish, and will raise wars, bloodshed, and the desolation of land and people for the sake of such *idol images*. All of these are a mere empty shell without fruit and belong to the fiery world for separation.

9. Men have brought it to this point: that the people *think* they are saved if they simply stick to the opinion of such men and support it. Whether they understand it or not, they think they are safe as long as they honor a <term>Sectarian Name</term> and hold the *patron* of their opinion to be right. When such a person hears the leader's name, he cries, "*Yes, yes, that is right*," and yet he does not know what it is. In this way, men have altogether blinded and seduced the simple, so that people look only at men's names and think Christ is found in the opinion. What is even worse, men are compelled by power into such image-like opinions. They have so blinded people that they will even forsake their bodies and goods for the sake of an opinion, which they do *not* fundamentally understand, and they persecute, hate, and kill one another for it.

10. Every one of them cries out that men will *take away the true doctrine, namely* the true faith, *from them*. And yet they do not possess it, nor is it found in their opinion. Thus, the world is entirely filled and blinded with opinions. Men suppose that if a person simply *uses* <term>Christ's Testaments</term> according to the opinion of his patron, then there is blessedness and salvation in it; otherwise, they think there can be *no* salvation. They believe that whoever does not visualize things according to that same opinion, or whoever does not cling and cleave to them, cannot be saved; they also believe he is no true member of the right <term>Christendom</term>.

11. Men contend so miserably about such image-like opinions that the churches are turned into nothing else but mere houses of contentious argument and spiritual dens of *murder*. This *murder* in the end leads to *wars* and *bloodshed*, and utter disgrace...

He laments that people are misled into following sectarian names and opinions rather than the living Christ, leading to social and political desolation.</summary>

# Of the Contention of the Learned, etc. Chapter 5.

...and the dishonor done to Christ for the sake of his holy gifts and Testaments <note>original: "Testaments" refers here to the sacraments, specifically the Holy Supper or Eucharist</note>; and in truth, nothing else is established by this, except as Israel danced about the golden calf and made an **idol calf to be their God**, joining in their own handiwork—namely, in their idol image—and lost their God. Therefore, the anger of God was also kindled against them and consumed them all in the wilderness, so that such servants of idols and images could not enter into the promised land.

12. Loving brethren, do not struggle over opinions; all contentious debate is the image of an idol. Concerning his omnipresence, Christ told us of no "opinion" where he says, *He will be with us every day to the end of the world* (Matthew 28:20). He does not say "in *such* or *such* an opinion," but where he indicates his presence, he says this: *As the lightning goes forth and shines even to its setting, so shall also the ever-enduring coming of the Son of Man be* (Matthew 24:27). And he says, *The Kingdom of God is within you* (Luke 17:21).

13. Christ's light and power rise up in his children in the *inward ground* <note>original: "inward ground" refers to the deep, spiritual center of the human soul</note> and shine to them through the *whole course* of their life; and in that fountain of light is the Kingdom of God *in man*. Now, if a person does not have this, let him argue and debate as much as he wants, yet he will never bring it into himself by any opinion. But if he has it, then *even streams of love* flow out from that same fountain; it needs no opinion. Let him only see to it that Christ's Kingdom is *born* in him—that Christ becomes man in him—otherwise he is no Christian, regardless of his opinions. He must stand as a branch in the vine of Christ (John 15). Opinion does not help him, but true faith does, which is active through the breaking forth of love *and performs good works* (Galatians 5:6). If he does not have the works of love, then he also has no faith. Opinion creates no salvation but is Babel <note>Babel: A biblical reference to the Tower of Babel, used here to mean a state of spiritual confusion and sectarian division</note>, a confusion of the languages of the one and only love. No one is a Christian unless he loves his neighbor and desires to do him good.

14. <margin>Or, Childlike.</margin> Outwardly imputed grace <note>original: "imputed grace" refers to the theological concept of Christ's righteousness being credited to a believer</note>, without innate filial grace, is entirely false. When Christ works in a person, then he is a Christian, and then the sufferings, merits, and satisfaction of Christ benefit him. When he has Christ within himself as an advocate who has accomplished it—so that he may also do it in him and draw his merits into him—then the Kingdom of God is in that *merit*; otherwise, all idol-like opinions are false. No work pleases God except what he himself works in man through *his Spirit*; therefore, let us be the children of Christ, and not the children of images.

15. Christ has shared his Kingdom with us in his Testaments; whoever wishes to receive it must be his child, otherwise there is no inheritance. To practice repentance is better than to desire to know much. If knowledge is not given by God to a person, then he will not be able to understand the basis of the divine secret mystery; but if it is given to him, he needs no "image" <note>in this context, an "image" refers to a mental construct or sectarian dogma</note>. To remain in the humility and simplicity of Christ, and to cling to his *love* and grace without despising anyone, is good Christianity. Whatever speaks only of itself is Babel; in *Christ* we are all members, and all one. *Amen.*

<header>Fig. II</header>

# THE CONSTITUENT PARTS OF MAN.

->The MIND of Man, when strictly considered only as it is in itself, can be most significantly called Man's "Nothing" and "All."<-
->The manifestation of the MIND of Man according to Darkness, Fire, and Light; without this manifestation, the MIND of Man is entirely unknown to and unaware of itself.<-

---

->The Three Constituent Parts of Man's Created Being.<-

<note>The diagram features a shaded sphere representing Darkness, a triangle inscribed with the word FIRE, and a sun-like circle inscribed with the word LIGHT. This visualizes the three states of the human soul described below.</note>

---

| **Hellish-Mindedness** | **Earthly-Mindedness** | **Heavenly-Mindedness** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Influenced by the three primary lower properties of the Dark World, where the Devil is the active power. | Influenced chiefly by the seven temporary <note>original: "temporal"</note> properties of the Spirit of this World, which is the active power there, though the Devil is not excluded. | Influenced by the Spirit of God, who is the active power in the Holy World of Light and Love. |

---

**[Hellish Disposition]**
> A disposition and will toward wickedness: such as to lie, to steal, to curse and swear, to murder, and so on.
> <center>The actual execution of this will, either in all or in some of these cursed things.</center>

**[Earthly Disposition]**
> A disposition and will to love this world and the things within it, its lusts, and so on.
> <center>The actual performance of this will, or a real love for this world and the things within it.</center>

**[Heavenly Disposition]**
> A disposition and will toward righteousness: to love God above all things, and your neighbor as yourself.
> <center>The bringing of this will into practice and deed; the real, practical love of God and neighbor.</center>

---

> Note here that although hellish-mindedness can exist in a soul (and does in many) without any mixture of heavenly-mindedness—and heavenly-mindedness can likewise exist without the hellish—neither of these two can exist without some mixture of earthly-mindedness. This is because this world is a perpetual mixture of good and evil. Therefore, the fact that these three are represented here as separate from each other does not mean they are so separate in any soul; rather, it means that one or the other is predominant in every soul. If either the heavenly or hellish state keeps its predominance until death separates the soul from the body, the result will be:

---

**[The End of the Hellish]**
> An inevitable downfall into <term>perdition</term> <note>Eternal ruin or damnation.</note>, where the worm does not die and the fire is not quenched.

**[The End of the Earthly]**
> A separation of good and evil, confining everything to that world from which it had its first origin.

**[The End of the Heavenly]**
> A rising up into life and happiness, which shall have a beginning but never any end.

---

<meta>This page serves as an editor's preface or "Advertisement" for the fourth volume of the works of Jakob Böhme (Jacob Behmen). It addresses the transition in editorship following the death of the previous supervisor and explains the sources used for the translations.</meta>

<sig>I</sig>

# NOTICE.

If the long delay of this volume—following the notice included in the last one, which might lead one to expect it sooner—seems to require an apology, the editor hopes that the following will be accepted as a reasonable explanation (among other less important reasons). The worthy person who directly supervised the publication of this accurate and valuable English edition of Jacob Behmen’s <note>original: "Jacob Behmen" refers to Jakob Böhme (1575–1624), a German Christian mystic and Lutheran theologian whose works had a profound influence on later philosophy and mysticism.</note> works passed away shortly after this book began printing. The difficult and important task of continuing the work fell to one of his close friends. While this friend does not lack the will to finish, he admits he is less capable than his predecessor in executing such a weighty responsibility. For this reason, he fears the quality of the book's presentation may require more of an excuse than the delay itself.

The various treatises collected in this volume are printed nearly exactly according to the original *English* translations from the 1600s <note>original: "the last Century"</note>, with a few exceptions. These exceptions include the book titled *The Way to Christ*, *The Treatise on the Four Complexions*, and the small tract *The Way from Darkness to True Illumination*. These specific treatises were recently reprinted by *T. Mills*, a bookseller in *Bristol*, in a neat pocket-sized volume. That version used a style better suited to the taste and understanding of *modern* <note>In this context, "modern" refers to the late 18th-century readership for whom the language was updated from the original 17th-century prose.</note> readers—a goal the Bristol editor claimed was for their spiritual benefit. The editor of this fourth volume has chosen to follow *that* edition for these specific texts rather than the old translation, hoping it will be more accessible and intelligible to sincere and simple-minded readers. Although that version differs in several places from the original 17th-century English version—and the editor admits it should be viewed as a *liberal* rather than *strictly literal* translation—he also hopes these variations will clarify, strengthen, or highlight the author’s meaning without damaging his overall sense, scope, or simplicity.

Aiming to benefit and satisfy the fair-minded and well-disposed reader, the editor of this volume has also included a translation (or rather, a paraphrase) of a portion of *Jacob Behmen’s* treatise *The Supersensual Life*. This was written by the late, respected *Mr. William Law* <note>William Law (1686–1761) was an influential Anglican priest and mystic. His later writings were heavily influenced by Böhme, and he is often associated with this specific multi-volume edition of Böhme's works, though it was actually completed by others after his death.</note> and was found as an original manuscript among the papers of the previous editor, who was known to be a very close friend of *Mr. Law*. The current editor has inserted this paraphrased translation in its proper place and marked it in a

Note <meta>catchword: Note</meta>

<summary>This preface explains the transition in editorship for the fourth volume of Jakob Böhme's works following the death of the previous editor. It details the decision to use more contemporary (18th-century) translations for certain treatises to improve readability for the general public.</summary>
<keywords>Jacob Behmen, Jakob Böhme, William Law, The Way to Christ, The Supersensual Life, translation, mysticism, T. Mills, Bristol, 18th-century publishing</keywords>

# ADVERTISEMENT

Regarding the note at the bottom of the 104th page, both where it begins and where it ends: the editor thinks it necessary—out of fairness to the author, the reader, and the truth—to acknowledge here the liberties taken with the author's original text. He hopes at the same time that the intended goal, which is the *spiritual* benefit and pleasure of the readers, will justify his actions so well that they will offer their thanks rather than feel the need to grant him a pardon.

Some of the diagrams <note>original: "Figures"</note> left by Mr. Law <note>William Law (1686–1761), an influential English theologian and mystic who edited and illustrated the works of Jacob Boehme</note>, which were designed to illustrate the works of this wonderful writer <note>Jacob Boehme (1575–1624), the German Christian mystic known as the "Teutonic Philosopher"</note>, were attached to the previous volumes; some are attached to this one, and others will accompany the volumes that follow. However, because no explanations for these diagrams were found (unlike those published in the last two volumes), none are or will be provided. 

It is hoped that this deficiency will be felt less strongly, and therefore be less a matter of just complaint, when one considers that the engravings <note>original: "Plates"</note> and their explanations already printed describe those *original* and *essential properties of eternal nature*, which are the *foundation* <note>original: "Ground"</note> of all created life and existence. It is assumed that whoever has gained a true and sufficient knowledge of these principles may have less need for help, and consequently regret the lack of further explanations less, when trying to understand the meaning and purpose of the diagrams added to this volume and those that will follow. This is because they all rely on the *principles* illustrated by the *engravings* and explained by the *descriptions* presented in the volumes mentioned above.

<summary>The editor acknowledges making changes to the original text for the reader's spiritual benefit and explains that while new illustrative diagrams by William Law are included, they lack specific written explanations because none were found in the archives.</summary>

# P R E F A C E

-> TO THE <-

## R E A D E R .

**T**HIS book is a true mystical mirror of the highest wisdom. The best treasure that a person can attain in this world is true knowledge—specifically, the knowledge of oneself. For man is the great mystery of God, the <term>microcosm</term> <note>A "microcosm" is a "little world" or a miniature representation of the entire universe.</note>, or the complete summary of the whole universe. He is the <note>original: "Mirandum Dei opus" — God’s marvelous work</note>, God's masterpiece, a living emblem and <term>Hieroglyphic</term> <note>A "hieroglyphic" here refers to a symbolic or sacred representation.</note> of eternity and time. Therefore, to know where he comes from, and what his temporal and eternal being and well-being are, must necessarily be that ONE essential thing toward which all our primary study should aim. In comparison to this, all the wealth of this world is but dross and a loss to us.

Hence Solomon, the wisest of the kings of Israel, says: *Happy is the man who finds wisdom, and the man who gets understanding; for the value of it is better than the value of silver, and the gain from it better than fine gold; she is more precious than rubies, and all things that can be desired are not to be compared to her.*

This is that wisdom which lives in nothing, and yet possesses all things; the humble, resigned soul is its companion. This is the divine <term>Alloquy</term> <note>original: "Alloquy" — a formal conversation or dialogue, here referring to God speaking directly to the soul.</note>, the inspiration of the Almighty, the breath of God, and the holy anointing which sanctifies the soul to be the temple of the Holy Spirit. It instructs the soul rightly in all things and searches <margin>ᵃ 1 Corinthians 2:10.</margin> the deep things of God <note>original Greek: τὰ βάθη τοῦ Θεοῦ</note>.

This is the precious pearl whose beauty is more glorious and whose power is more effective than the sun. It is a never-failing comfort in all afflictions, a balsam for all sores, a <term>panacea</term> <note>A universal remedy or cure-all.</note> for all diseases, and a sure antidote against all poison and death itself. It is that joyful and assured companion and guide which never forsakes a person, but escorts him through this valley of misery and death into the blessed paradise of perfect bliss.

If you ask, "What is the way to attain this wisdom?" Behold! Christ, who is the Way, the Truth, and the Life, tells you plainly in these words: *If anyone desires to follow me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily* <margin>ᵇ Luke 9:23.</margin> *and follow me;* or as he says elsewhere, *Unless you are born again, you cannot see the kingdom of heaven;* or as St. Paul says, <margin>ᶜ 1 Corinthians 3:18.</margin> *If anyone among you seems to be wise in this world, let him become a fool so that he may be wise.*

## The PREFACE.

In this lies that simple, child-like way to the highest wisdom, which no sharp-witted reason or worldly learning can reach. Indeed, it is foolishness to human reasoning, and therefore so few take the path to find it. The proud sophists and "wise-lings" <note>original: "Wiselings" — those who think themselves wise but lack true insight.</note> of this world have always trampled it underfoot with scorn and contempt. They have called it enthusiasm <note>original: "Enthusiasm" — in this period, the word often implied fanatical or irrational religious delusion.</note>, madness, melancholy, whimsy, fancy, and so on; but wisdom is justified by her children.

Indeed, not everyone is suited for or capable of knowing the eternal and temporal nature in its mysterious operations. Nor is the proud, greedy world worthy to receive a clear manifestation of it. Therefore, the only wise God (who gives wisdom to everyone who asks it of him correctly) has locked up the jewel in his blessed treasury, which none can open except those who have the key. That key is this: *Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you.* The Father will give the Spirit to those who ask him for it.

This is the true theosophical <term>theosophy: A system of belief that seeks direct knowledge of the divine through spiritual intuition and contemplation.</term> school where this author learned the first rudiments and principles of wisdom, and to which we must go if we wish to understand his deep writings. For we must recognize that the sons of *Hermes* <note>original: "Sons of Hermes" — followers of Hermeticism, a philosophical tradition based on writings attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, focusing on the relationship between the human and the divine.</note>, who have graduated from the high school of true magic and theosophy, have always spoken their hidden wisdom as a mystery. They have so embedded it under shadows and figures, parables and similes, that no one can understand their obscure (yet clear) writings except those who have been admitted into the same school and have tasted the feast of Pentecost <note>A reference to the Holy Spirit granting the gift of tongues and understanding to the apostles.</note>.

And this does not seem at all strange to the children of divine *Mercury* <note>In this context, Mercury refers to the "spirit" or the communicative power that bridges the human and the divine.</note>. For the mysteries of philosophy, divinity, and theosophy must not be profaned or laid open to the view of the outward astral reason <term>astral reason: Human intelligence that is tied to the physical cosmos and the senses, rather than spiritual revelation.</term>. Such reason turns everything toward its own selfish pride, greed, envy, wrath, and cunning hypocrisy. Therefore, a parabolical or "magical" phrase or dialect is the best and plainest garment and dress that mysteries can wear to travel up and down this wicked world. Thus, parables have a double and different purpose: they conceal and hide secrets from the rude and vulgar sort, who are neither able nor patient enough to endure anything that does not suit their common conceits and opinions; yet they also sweetly lead the mind of the true seeker into the depths of wisdom's counsel. They are like the cloudy pillar of *Moses*: they have a dark part and a light part. They are dark to the Egyptians—the pharisaical sons of sophistry—but light to the true Israel, the children of the mystery.

Therefore, whoever wishes to be nurtured and trained by *Sophia* <term>Sophia: The personification of Divine Wisdom, often viewed in mystical traditions as the feminine aspect of God.</term> and learn to understand and speak the language of wisdom must be born again of and in the Word of Wisdom, *Christ Jesus*, the immortal seed. The divine essence which God breathed into his paradisaical soul must be revived. He must become one again with that which he was in God before he was a created being. Then his eternal spirit may enter into that which is within the veil, and see not only the literal, but also the moral, allegorical, and anagogical <note>original: "anagogical" — the spiritual or mystical sense of a text that points toward the afterlife or eternity.</note> meanings of the wise and their dark sayings. He then will be fit to enter not only into *Solomon's Porch*—the outer court of natural philosophy, sense, and reason—but likewise into the inward court of holy and spiritual exercises in divine understanding and knowledge. In this way, he may step into the most inward and holiest...

In this work, the author fundamentally explains the birth, sympathy, and antipathy of all beings. He provides a clear and manifest demonstration of how man has turned himself away from good and into evil, and how his transformation <note>original: "Transmutation"</note> can lead him back from evil into good.

# SIGNATURA RERUM;
### THE
# SIGNATURE of all THINGS.

### The First Chapter.

<margin>d The Being of all beings.</margin>
*How everything spoken of God without knowledge of the "signature" is mute and lacks understanding; and how the signature lies precisely composed within the human mind according to the <sup>d</sup> essence of all essences.*

1. Everything that is spoken, written, or taught about God without the knowledge of the signature is mute and void of understanding. It proceeds only from historical guesswork <term>original: historical conjecture; knowledge based on external reports or tradition rather than internal spiritual experience</term>, coming from the mouth of another person where the spirit remains silent because it lacks direct knowledge. But if the Spirit reveals the signature to a person, then he understands the speech of another. Furthermore, he understands how the Spirit has manifested and revealed itself (from the essence through the underlying principle) in the sound of the voice. Even if I see someone speak, teach, preach, and write of God, and even if I hear and read those things, this is not enough for me to truly understand him. However, if his sound and spirit—coming from his own signature and likeness—enter into my own likeness <term>original: similitude; the internal image or corresponding form within a person</term> and imprint his image into mine, then I may understand him truly and fundamentally (whether through speech or writing), provided he has the hammer that can strike my bell <note>This famous metaphor from Boehme suggests that true communication requires a spiritual resonance between the speaker's internal state and the listener's internal state.</note>.

2. By this we know that all human qualities proceed from one source—that they all have only one root and mother. Otherwise, one person could not understand another through sound; for through sound or speech, a form marks and imprints itself into the likeness of another. A similar tone or sound catches and moves another, and within that sound, the spirit imprints its own likeness, which it has conceived in its essence and brought to form in the underlying principle.

<margin>e Or, formed itself; or originally put forth itself.</margin>
3. Thus, through the word, one can understand what the spirit has conceived <sup>e</sup>, whether in good or evil. With this signature, the spirit enters into another person's form and awakens a similar form within that person's signature. Consequently, both forms mutually harmonize into one form, resulting in one comprehension, one will, one spirit, and also one understanding.

He explains that human communication is possible because all people share a single spiritual root, allowing one person's internal "form" to awaken a similar "signature" in another.</summary>

# Signatura Rerum: Chapter 1.

4. And then secondly we understand that the *Signature* or **Form** is not the Spirit itself, but the **receptacle, container, or cabinet of the Spirit** where it resides; for the *Signature* exists in the *Essence* <note>original: "Essence"; here referring to the fundamental substance or being of a thing</note> and is like a *lute* <note>a stringed instrument</note> that remains still. It is indeed a silent thing that is neither heard nor understood, but if it is played upon, then its **Form** is understood—revealing the state and tune in which it stands, and according to which note it is set. Likewise, the *Signature* of *Nature* in its **Form** is a silent *Essence*; it is like a prepared *musical instrument* upon which the *Will’s Spirit* plays; whichever strings he touches, they sound according to their particular quality.

5. In the human *Mind*, the *Signature* lies most skillfully composed, according to the *Essence* of all *Essences*; and *Man* lacks nothing but the wise *Master* who can strike his *instrument*, which is the true *Spirit* of the high *Might* of *Eternity*. If that is quickened in *Man*, so that it stirs and acts in the *center* of the *mind*, then it plays on the *instrument* of the human **Form**, and only then is the **Form** <margin>f Proceeds from the mouth.</margin> expressed with the *sound* in the **Word**. As his *instrument* was tuned during the time of his <margin>g Or, Conception.</margin> **Incarnation**, so it sounds, and such is his *knowledge*; the inner self manifests itself in the *sound* of the **Word**, for that is the *Mind’s* natural *knowledge* of itself.

6. *Man* indeed has all the *Forms* of all three *Worlds* <note>Boehme’s cosmology consists of three "worlds" or principles: the dark world (fire/wrath), the light world (love/spirit), and the outer world (nature/materiality).</note> residing within him; for he is a complete image of God, or of the Being of all beings. However, the order is established in him at his **Incarnation**; for there are three "Work-masters" in him who prepare his **Form** [or Signature], namely the threefold *Fiat* <note>Latin: "let it be done"; the creative command of God</note> according to the three *Worlds*. They are in *contest* over the **Form**, and the **Form** is shaped according to this *contest*. Whichever *Master* holds the dominant rule and gains control in the *Essence*, the *instrument* is tuned according to him, while the others remain hidden and fall behind with their *sound*, as is plainly seen.

7. As soon as *Man* is born into this *world*, his *spirit* plays upon his *instrument*, so that his innate, genuine **Form** [or Signature]—whether good or evil—is seen through his words and behavior. For as his *instrument* sounds, the senses and thoughts proceed accordingly from the *Essence* of the *Mind*; thus the external *spirit* of the *Will* is expressed in its behavior, as can be seen in both men and beasts. There is a great difference in procreation, such that one brother or sister does not act like the other.

8. Furthermore, we must know that although one *Fiat* maintains the upper hand and shapes the **Form** according to itself, the other two still give their *sound* if their *instrument* is played upon. It is seen that many a *man*, and also many a *beast*, though very much inclined toward either good or evil, may be moved to the opposite by a contrary tune. They often let their inbred *Signature* [or figure] fall when a contrary *tune* is played upon their hidden *lute* or **Form**. For instance, we see that an evil *man* is often moved by a good *man* to repent and cease from his iniquity when the good *man* touches and strikes the evil man's hidden *instrument* with his own meek and loving *spirit*.

9. In the same way, it happens to a good *man* that when a wicked *man* strikes his hidden *instrument* with a *spirit* of *wrath*, the **form** of *anger* is also stirred up in the good *man*. Thus one is set against the other, so that one might be the cure and healer of the other. For as the vital *Signature*—that is, the **Form** of Life—is shaped at the time of the *Fiat* during **conception**, so too is its natural *spirit*; for it arises out of the *Essence* of all three principles, and it acts and manifests a *Will* out of its own property.

10. But now the *Will* may be broken; for when a stronger force comes and raises a person's inward *Signature* with its own introduced *sound* and *Will-spirit*, then the original dominant ruler loses its power, right, and authority. We see this in the powerful influence of the *Sun*: by its strength, it transforms a bitter and sour fruit, turning it into sweetness and pleasantness. In the same way, a good *man* may be corrupted among evil company, and a good herb cannot fully show its real, genuine virtue in a bad...

11. And now observe: as a thing stands in the power and predominance of its quality, so it is signed and marked externally in its outward form, signature, or figure. A man is known by his speech, will, and behavior, as well as by the form of the members which he has and must use according to that signature; his inward form is noted in the $^h$ form of his face and $^i$ his look. Thus also it is with a beast, a herb, and the trees; everything—as it is inwardly [in its innate or <term>physiognomy</term> <note>original: "Phyfio-gnomy"; here referring to the internal nature or constitution</note> <margin>Physiognomy.</margin> virtue and quality]—is so signed outwardly. And though it often happens that a thing is changed from evil into good, or from good into evil, yet it still carries its external character so that the good or evil [that is, the change] may be known.

12. For a man is known by his daily practice, as well as by his conduct and conversation; for the "upper instrument," which is most strongly drawn, is always the one played upon <note>Boehme uses a musical metaphor here: the dominant part of a person's nature is like the primary string of an instrument that dictates the melody of their life.</note>. This is also the case with a beast that is wild; but when it is over-awed and tamed, and brought to another property, it does not easily show its first innate form unless it is stirred up, and then that original nature breaks forth and appears above all other forms.

13. It is likewise the same with the herbs of the earth; if a herb is transplanted out of a bad soil into a good one, it soon gains a stronger body and a more pleasant smell and power, showing the inward essence externally. There is nothing created or born in Nature that does not also manifest its internal form externally, for the internal continually labors or works itself toward manifestation. We see this in the power and form of this world—how the one and only essence has manifested itself within the external birth in the desire for <term>similitude</term> <note>original: "Similitude"; likeness or reflection of the divine</note>; how it has manifested itself in so many forms and shapes which we see and know in the stars and elements, as well as in living creatures, trees, and herbs.

<margin>i In.</margin>
14. Therefore, the greatest understanding lies in the "signature," wherein man (who is the image of the greatest virtue) may not only learn to know himself, but may also learn to know the essence of all essences. For $^i$ by the external form of all $^i$ creatures—by their instigation, inclination, and desire, as well as by their sound, voice, and speech—the hidden spirit is known. Nature has given to everything its language according to its essence and form; for the language or sound arises out of the essence, and the <term>Fiat</term> <note>Latin: "let it be done"; the creative command of God</note> of that essence forms the quality of the essence into the voice or virtue which it sends forth: to the animals in their sound, and to the $^k$ essential things <margin>k Vegetables.</margin> in their smell, virtue, and form.

For each thing manifests its "mother" <note>In Boehme's thought, the "mother" refers to the source, matrix, or essential origin from which a thing is born.</note>, which gives the essence and the will to the form.

## The Second Chapter.

### Of the Opposition and Combat in the Essence of all Essences, through which the Basis of Antipathy and Sympathy in Nature may be seen, and also the Corruption and Cure of every Thing.

1. <image-desc>An ornate woodcut initial 'S' containing an inner 'S' surrounded by various symbols: a sun/Sol symbol (circle with dot), a moon/Luna crescent, a lion (Leo), and other alchemical or astrological signs.</image-desc> Since there are so many diverse forms, each always producing a different will from its own property <note>original: "Property"; in Boehme's philosophy, this refers to the inherent quality or characteristic "signature" of a thing</note>, we understand from this the conflict and combat within the Being of all beings. We see how one form opposes, poisons, and kills another—that is, it overcomes the other's essence and the spirit of that essence—and forces it into another form. This is the source of sickness and pain: when one essence destroys another.

2. From this, we also understand the cure: how one thing heals another and restores it to health. If this conflict did not exist, there would be no Nature, but only an eternal stillness and no will. For it is the opposing will that creates motion and the origin of "seeking," where the opposing sound seeks rest, yet in that seeking, it only elevates and further ignites itself.

<margin>Made sick.</margin>
3. We must understand that the cure for everything lies in the *assimilate* <note>original: "Aſſimulate"; something of a similar nature or likeness. Boehme follows the alchemical principle of "like cures like"</note>. In the *assimilate*, the will finds its satisfaction—that is, its highest joy. Every thing desires a will like its own and is distressed by an opposing will. But if it obtains a will of its own likeness, it rejoices in that similarity and settles into rest; thus, enmity is turned into joy.

4. For Eternal Nature has produced nothing in its desire except a likeness of itself. If there were not an everlasting mixing, there would be eternal peace in Nature; however, Nature would then remain unrevealed and hidden. It is through combat that Nature becomes manifest. Each thing elevates itself, trying to escape the combat and reach quiet rest; in doing so, it runs back and forth, which only awakens and stirs up the combat further. <margin>X</margin>

5. We clearly see by the light of nature <note>The "light of nature" refers to the innate or divine understanding accessible through observing the natural world</note> that there is no better help or remedy for this opposition—and no higher cure—than liberty, which is the desire of the spirit.

6. Furthermore, we find that an essence cannot be better remedied than with the *assimilate*. Because the essence is a "being," its desire is for "being." Every taste desires only its own kind; if it obtains it, its hunger is satisfied, appeased, and eased. It ceases to hunger and rejoices in itself, whereby the sickness settles into a state of rest because the hunger of the conflict ceases to work.

7. Since human life consists of <insert>three principles</insert>—that is, a threefold essence—it also has a threefold spirit derived from the property of each essence. First, there is the spirit according to eternal nature and the property of fire. Second, there is the spirit according to the property of eternal light and divine essentiality. Third, there is the spirit according to the property of the outward world. Therefore, we must consider the property of this threefold spirit, as well as this threefold essence and will: how each spirit, along with its essence, enters into strife and sickness, and what its cure and remedy may be.

8. We understand that beyond Nature, there is an eternal stillness and rest—namely, the <insert>Nothing</insert>. We also understand that an eternal will arises within that Nothing to turn the Nothing into Something, so that the will might find, feel, and behold itself.

<summary>Boehme explains that natural existence is defined by a conflict of wills (antipathy), which causes sickness, while healing is achieved through "the assimilate" (sympathy or likeness). He introduces the "three principles" of human life and describes the origin of "Something" from the eternal "Nothing" through the action of the will.</summary>

9. For in the "Nothing" <note>Böhme uses "the Nothing" to describe the Ungrund, or the state of pure potential before God or the universe manifests.</note>, the Will would not be revealed to itself. Therefore, we know that the Will seeks itself and finds itself within itself. Its seeking is a **Desire**, and its finding is the **Essence** of that Desire in which the Will finds itself.

10. It finds nothing except the quality of "Hunger," which is itself. It draws this hunger into itself—that is, it draws itself into itself—and finds itself within itself. This attraction into itself creates a shadowing or Darkness within it, which does not exist in the "Liberty" (that is, in the Nothing). For the Will of the Liberty shadows itself with the Essence of the Desire, because it is the Desire that creates Essence, not the Will.

11. Now, the fact that the Will must exist in Darkness is its own contradiction. It conceives within itself another Will to emerge from the Darkness back into the Liberty (the Nothing). Yet it cannot reach the Liberty from outside itself, because the Desire moves outward, causing a Source <note>original: "Source" – in Böhme’s terminology, this often refers to a "Qual," a surging fountain of sensation or suffering.</note> and Darkness. Therefore, the Will—specifically, the newly conceived Will—must turn inward, and yet there is no separation.

12. For within itself, before the Desire exists, there is the Liberty (the Nothing). Yet the Will cannot remain a "Nothing" because it desires to reveal itself within the Nothing. Still, no revelation can be achieved except through the Essence of the Desire. The more the newly conceived Will desires to be revealed, the more strongly and eagerly the Desire draws into itself. This creates three Forms within it: first, the **Desire**, which is contracting <note>original: "astringent"</note> and creates Hardness, for it is an enclosing from which Coldness arises. This attraction causes <margin>Or, Sting.</margin> a stinging agitation <note>original: "Compunction"</note> and movement within the Hardness—a conflict against the contracted Hardness. This attraction is the second Form, the cause of motion and life. It stirs within the contraction and hardness, which the "Enclosing" <margin>Contraction, or tightening.</margin> cannot tolerate. Therefore, it pulls even more eagerly to contain the stinging, which only makes the stinging stronger.

13. Thus, the stinging sensation strives upward and whirls crosswise, yet it cannot escape because the Hardness (the Desire) stays and detains it. Therefore, it remains like a triangle or a rotating sphere. Since it cannot move from its place, it begins to wheel, which creates a mixing within the Desire—the "Essence" or the diversity of the Desire. This turning creates a constant confusion and friction <note>original: "Contrition"</note>, from which arises the third Form: **Anguish** (the pain or the "sting of sense").

14. But as the Desire (the contraction) becomes even stronger through this process—since wrath and nature (motion) arise from the agitation—the original Will toward Desire becomes completely harsh <note>original: "austere"</note> and hungry. It exists in a hard, stinging, dry Essence and cannot escape it, for the Will itself creates this Essence and possesses it. <margin>Love and Anger, Father and Son.</margin> Thus, the Will now finds itself moved from "Nothing" into "Something." Yet this "Something" is contrary to its original Will, for it is a state of unrest, whereas the Free-will is stillness.

15. This is the origin of conflict: that "Nature" opposes the Free-will, and a thing is at war with itself. Here we understand the "Center of Nature" with its three forms. In the "first principle" <note>The realm of God’s power or the "dark" fire.</note>, it is *Spirit*; in the second <note>The realm of Light, Love, and Christ.</note>, it is *Love*; and in the third principle <note>The physical, material world.</note>, it is *Essence*. These three forms are called in the third principle *Sulphur, Mercury,* and *Salt* <note>original: "Sal."</note>.

16. Understand it this way: ***Sul*** in the first principle is the Free-will, or the "Inward Longing" <note>original: "Lubet" – from the German *Lust* or *Liebe*, meaning a divine inclination, delight, or "pleasurable attraction."</note> to move from Nothing to Something; it exists in "Liberty" without "Nature." ***Phur*** is the Desire of that free Longing. In the *Phur* (the Desire), it creates an Essence. This Essence is harsh because of the attraction, leading it into the three forms mentioned above and eventually into the fourth form, which is **Fire**. In *Phur*, we understand the origin of both eternal and external Nature, for "Hardness" is the mother and preserver of the sharpness of all essences. Out of *Sul* (the longing for Liberty), the dark Anguish becomes a shining Light. In the third principle (the outward kingdom), *Sul* is the "Oil of Nature," in which life burns and everything grows.

<summary>Böhme describes the mystical process by which the divine "Will" moves from "Nothing" into "Something," creating the "Center of Nature" through three forms of desire and anguish. He explains the alchemical trinity of Sulphur, Mercury, and Salt as manifestations of these spiritual principles.</summary>

## Signatura Rerum: Chapter 2.

17. But now the *Phur* <note>original: "Phur," representing the fire or the anxious desire within the word "Sulphur."</note>, which is the *Desire*, is not divided from *Sul* <note>original: "Sul," representing the light or the "oil" of the divine liberty.</note>; it is one word, one origin, and one essence. However, it separates itself into two properties: joy and sorrow, light and darkness. It creates two worlds: a dark fire-world in its severity, and a light fire-world in the *Lubet* <note>original: "Lubet," a term used by Boehme to describe a pleasing desire, a divine longing, or the "will" toward manifestation.</note> of liberty. For this *Lubet* of liberty is the only reason the fire shines; the original fire is dark and black. Within the shining of the fire, the Deity is understood; and within the dark fire—that is, in the source of anguish—the origin of nature is understood. In this, we further understand the "cure" <note>Boehme uses "cure" to mean the balancing, healing, or reconciliation of opposing forces.</note>.

18. This source of tension is the cure for the free *Lubet*—that is, for the still eternity. The stillness finds itself alive within it; it brings itself through the source of anguish into life, namely into the Kingdom of Joy. Thus, the "Nothing" has become an eternal life and has found itself, which could not happen in the stillness.

19. Secondly, we find that the *Sul*—the *Lubet* of liberty—is the curer of the *Desire*, which is the anxious nature. For the luster of liberty shines again (from the fire ignited out of nature) into the dark anguish, filling or satisfying the anguish with liberty. By this, the wrath is extinguished, and the *Turning Orb* <note>original: "Turning Orb," referring to the restless "wheel of nature" or the cycle of the first three properties of nature.</note> stands still; instead of the turning, a sound is produced within the essence.

20. This is the form of the spiritual life and of the essential life. *Sul* is the origin of the joyful life, and *Phur* is the origin of the essential life. The *Lubet* exists before and outside of nature, and this is the true *Sul*. The Spirit is made manifest in nature through the "source" <note>the point of tension or boiling over</note>, appearing in a two-fold form: according to the *Lubet* of liberty in a source of joy, and according to the anxious desire's *Lubet*. In the latter, it is—according to its astringency—piercing, bitter, and envious from its own stinging; and according to the anguish of the "wheel," it is entirely murderous and hateful. Each property dwells in itself, and yet they are within one another. In this, God’s love and anger are understood; they dwell in each other, and one does not seize the other, yet each is the curer of the other. This must be understood through *Imagination*, for the *Eternal* is *Magical*.

21. The second form in nature, in eternity, is the *Orb* with its piercing, bitter essences. For here the essence arises—understand this as arising with perturbation <note>disturbance or agitation</note>. The "Nothing" is still and without motion, but this perturbation makes the Nothing active. But in the third principle <note>the physical or outward world</note>—that is, in the dominion of the essence and the source of the outward world—the form is called Mercury. This Mercury is opposite, hateful, and poisonous; it is the cause of life and movement, and also the cause of the senses. Here, a single <gloss>p</gloss> glance <note>the "p" likely refers to "point" or "punctum"</note> may conceive itself within infinity and then immerse itself into it, where from one single point, an abyssal, unsearchable, and infinite multiplicity may arise.

22. This form is unquietness, yet it is also the seeker of rest. With its seeking, it causes unquietness, making itself its own enemy. Its cure is twofold because its desire is also twofold: according to the *Lubet* of liberty (striving for stillness and meekness), and according to the hunger for the rising of unquietness (the finding of itself). The root desires only joy with its first will, and yet it cannot obtain it except through the opposite source; for no joy can arise in the still Nothing. <insert>It must arise only through motion and elevation so that the Nothing finds itself.</insert> <margin><image-desc>A hand-drawn symbol of a cross or asterisk within a circle.</image-desc></margin>

23. Now, that which is found desires to enter again into the will of the still Nothing, so that it may have peace and rest there. The "Nothing" is its cure. Yet the wrath and poison are the remedies of the seeker and finder; that is the life they find. We see an example of this in the poisonous gall <note>bile</note>, from which joy and sorrow arise in life. In this, we also understand a twofold will: one toward the wrathful fire and the anxious, painful life (the origin of nature), and one toward the light-life—the joy of nature—which takes its origin out of the eternal Nothing.

24. The first Will's cure is the *Lubet* <term>original: "Lubet"; a term used by Boehme to describe a divine longing, delight, or inclination</term> of Liberty; if it attains that, it creates triumphant joy within itself. The wrath in the hungry desire is the curer and helper of the other Will—namely, the Will of Nature. Here, God's love and anger are understood, as well as how evil and good exist in the center ^q of every life, how no joy could arise without sorrow, and how one is the healer of the other.

<margin>Or, Voices.</margin>
25. And here we understand the third Will (which takes its origin out of both of these—namely, out of such an essence, or out of the "Mother"), which is the Spirit. This Spirit has both of these properties within it and is a "Son" of the properties as well as a Lord over them. For the power resides in him; he may awaken whichever property he pleases. The properties lie within the essence and are like a well-tuned instrument with many ^r strings that are currently still. The Spirit—namely, the "Egress" <note>original: "Egress"; the outflowing or emergence of the will into action</note>—is the real life; he may play upon the instrument as he pleases, in evil or good, according to love or anger. As he plays, and as the instrument sounds, so is it received by its "contra-tenor" <note>original: "contra-tenor"; a musical term for a counter-part or corresponding harmony</note>—namely, by that which is like-natured to it.

26. If the tune of love is played—that is, the desire of Liberty—then the sound is received by that same Liberty and love-*Lubet*. For it is its pleasing relish, agreeable to the desire of its will; one similar *Lubet* attracts another.

27. And it is to be understood the same way regarding enmity and the contrary will. If the instrument is struck according to the desire for Nature—that is, in wrath, anger, and bitter falsehood—then that same contrary sound and wrathful desire receives it. This is because it matches its own property and is a satisfying of its hunger. Here we understand the desire of both the Light World and the Dark World—a two-fold source and property.

<margin>Or, God.</margin>
28. The desire of Liberty is meek, easy, and pleasant, and it is called ^s Good. The desire toward Nature makes itself dark, dry, hungry, and wrathful within itself; this is called God's anger and the "Dark World," which is the First Principle. The "Light World" is the Second Principle.

29. And we are to understand that it is no divided essence; rather, one holds the other hidden or enclosed within it. One is the beginning and cause of the other, as well as its healing and cure. Whichever is awakened and stirred up gains dominion and manifests itself externally with its "character," making a form and "signature" according to its will in the external world. We see a likeness <note>original: "Similitude"</note> of this in an enraged man or beast; although the outward man and beast are not in the inward world, the outward nature ^t still possesses those same forms. This is because it arises originally from the ^u inward world and stands upon that inward root.

30. The third form is "Anxiousness" <note>often translated as "Anguish" in Boehme's system</note>, which arises in Nature from the first and second forms and is the upholder or preserver of both. In itself, it is the sharp *Fiat* <note>Latin: "let it be done"; the creative command of God</note>. The second form possesses the *Verbum* <note>Latin: "the Word"</note>—that is, the property of the Word—and it consists of three properties. Out of herself and those three, she creates the fourth: Fire. In the external birth—that is, in the Third Principle—it is called *Sal* <note>Latin: "Salt"; an alchemical principle of physical stability</note> or Salt, according to its matter. But in its spirit, it has many forms, for it is the "Fire-Root," the great anguish. It arises between and out of the "astringency" <note>the force of contraction or drawing together</note> and bitterness in the harsh attraction. It is the essentiality of that which is attracted—the corporality or tangibility. From "Sulphur," it is of a brimstone nature, and from "Mercury," it is a blaze or flash. It is painful in itself, a "sharpness of dying" caused by the sharp attraction of the astringency. It has a two-fold fire: one cold, another hot. The cold arises from the astringency and the sharp attraction, and it is a dark, black fire. The hot fire arises from the driving forth of the "compunction" <margin>or sting of instigation</margin> ^x in the anguish of the desire for Liberty. Liberty is its enkindler, and the raging compunction is the ^y awakener <margin>raiser, enkindler, or enflamer</margin> of the cold fire.

31. These three forms are within one another as one, and yet they are only one. But they separate themselves through their origin into many forms, and yet they still have only one Mother.

32. Now we are to consider the hunger of the Anxiety <note>original: "Anguish"—Böhme uses this term to describe the agonizing, contractive tension at the root of existence</note>, or the Salt-Spirit, and how it is satisfied or fulfilled. This Anguish contains two Wills, originating from the first Will’s emergence from the "Liberty" <note>the divine freedom or "Ungrund" existing before creation</note> toward its own manifestation. Specifically, the first Will is directed toward Nature; the other, reconceived Will is the "Son" of the first, which exits the manifestation and returns into itself, back into the Liberty. It has become an eternal Life within Nature, yet it does not possess Nature as its essence; instead, it dwells within itself and penetrates Nature like a transparent <margin>Or, Out of itself.</margin> shining. 33. Thus, it has two properties: through its inward seeking, it creates the Center of Nature. This is like a poison, a Will of terrifying ambition, like a lightning bolt or a thunderclap. This Desire seeks only Anguish and horror, wanting to find itself within itself—moving from the "Nothing" into the "Something." 34. We understand the "Center" within itself—with its ambitious wrath and its wrathful Will toward Nature—to be the **Dark World**. We understand the "Egress" <note>exit or moving out</note> from itself toward Manifestation to be the **Outward World**. 35. The Desire of the Dark World is for manifestation—that is, for the Outward World—so that it may attract and draw that same "Essentiality" into itself to satisfy its wrathful hunger. Conversely, the Desire of the Outward World is for the Essence or Life that arises from the pain and Anguish.

36. Its internal Desire is the "Wonder of Eternity," a Mystery, or a Mirror; it is that which is grasped by the first Will toward Nature.

This is the essence it contains: a hunger for itself that is also its own satisfaction. For *Sul* desires *Phur*, and *Phur* desires *Mercury*, and both of these desire *Sal*. *Sal* is their "Son," whom they hatch through their Desire, and who afterward becomes their dwelling place and their food.

38. Every Desire seeks only the essence of <term>Salt</term> according to its own property, for Salt is diverse. others, for they are all four enkindled in the penetrating <term>Flagrat</term> <note>original: "Flagrat"; an alchemical term for a sudden burst of fire or energy, often associated with a spiritual flash or realization.</note>. This is followed by hail and rain. The hail forms within the coldness, in the property of the cold Salt-spirit; for the "Wrath" <note>Boehme uses "Wrath" to describe the contractive, harsh force of nature.</note> attracts itself and turns the water to ice. This water arises from "Meekness"—namely, from the desire of the Light—for water is the essential substance of meekness. The cold Salt-spirit congeals this into drops and distills it upon the earth; before this congealing, it exists only as a mist, steam, vapor, or dampness.

40. We see this process very exactly and properly in thunder and lightning. The flash—the lightning or ethereal blaze—always goes first, for it is the ignited <term>Salniter</term> <note>original: "Salniter"; saltpeter, which Boehme uses to represent the explosive, volatile power of the spirit in nature.</note>. Then follows the strike in the <term>Flagrat</term> of the coldness. As you can see, as soon as the strike occurs, the astringent chamber is opened, and a cool wind follows, often with whirling and wheeling. This happens because the forms of nature are awakened and act like a turning wheel, and so they carry their spirit, which is the wind.

# The Third Chapter

## Of the Grand Mystery of All Beings

1. Courteous Reader, observe the meaning correctly: by this description, we do not mean a "beginning" of the Deity. Instead, we show you the manifestation of the Deity through nature. For God is without beginning, and yet has an eternal beginning and an eternal end, which He is Himself. The nature of the inward world has existed in the same essence from eternity.

<margin>a <term>Mysterium</term> <note>original: "Mysterium"; the "Great Mystery," the hidden source of all existence.</note></margin>
2. We give you this to understand regarding the Divine Essence: without nature, God is a **a** <term>Mysterium</term>. Understand this as the "Nothing," for outside of nature is the Nothing, which is an Eye of Eternity—an eye of the <term>Abyss</term> <note>original: "Abyss"; Boehme's "Ungrund," the bottomless void or groundless source from which God originates.</note> that exists or sees in the Nothing. This same Eye is a Will—understand it as a longing for manifestation, to find the Nothing. But since there is nothing before the Will where it might find something or have a place to rest, it enters into itself and finds itself through Nature.

<margin>b Similitude, Likeness, or <term>Signature</term> <note>original: "Signature"; the outward sign or form that reveals an inner spiritual reality.</note></margin>
3. Within the Mystery without nature, we understand two forms in the first Will: the first is toward nature, for the manifestation of the "Wonder-Eye"; and the second form is produced out of the first, which is a desire for virtue and power. This is the first Will’s "Son," its desire for joyfulness. Understand us in this way: the Desire proceeds outward, and that which proceeds is the Spirit of the Will and Desire, for it is a moving force. This Desire creates a **b** form in the Spirit—namely, the formations of the infinity of the Mystery.

4. And this form (or likeness) is the eternal Wisdom of the Deity. In this, we understand the Trinity of the one Deity. We must not seek to know the ultimate ground of how the first Will arises in the Abyss from eternity (which is called the Father); we only know the eternal birth. We distinguish the Deity—namely, what purely and merely concerns the Deity, or the Good—from Nature. We show you the <term>Arcanum</term> <note>original: "Arcanum"; a profound secret or hidden mystery.</note> of the greatest secret mystery: namely, how the Abyss, or the Deity, manifests itself with this eternal generation. For God is a Spirit, as subtle as a thought or a will, and Nature is His corporeal essence—understand this as the Eternal Nature, as well as the outward nature of this visi-

This luster is, and causes, a Kingdom of Joy in the Liberty. Understand us thus: that the spirit's dominion—namely, the spirit and the essence—do thus separate.

This also becomes material in the bitter impression and divides itself in the separation: one part into brimstone, another into Salniter, and a third into a salty sharpness.
