38. *Mercury* is the <gloss>q</gloss> moving life in all things, and his mother is *Sulphur*. Now, life and death lie in *Sulphur*—namely, in the struggling *Mercurial* wheel. In the *Sulphur* there is fire, light, and darkness. The "impression" <note>In Boehme’s thought, "impression" refers to the spiritual force of contraction or compression that creates density.</note> causes darkness, coldness, and hardness, as well as great anguish. From the "impression" of this attraction, *Mercury* takes his rise; he is the sting of the attraction—the motion or disquietude—and he arises in the great anguish of the impression. In this state, a dark, cold fire arises in the impression because of the hardness; and in the sting of anguish—the disquietude—a hot fire arises.

### Chap. 13. The Signature of all Things.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "three principles" (Sulphur, Mercury, and Salt) as they relate to the spiritual and physical constitution of nature and the human body. Note that the original text skips from paragraph 43 to 45.</meta>

39. Now <term>Mercury</term><note>original: "Mercury"; in Böhme’s alchemy, Mercury represents the "Wheel of Motion"—the active, stirring, and communicative force in both spirit and matter.</note> is the Wheel of Motion and a stirring up of both the Cold and the Heat. In this state, it is only a painful, aching source of heat and cold—specifically, a cold and hot fiery "poison-anguish" that drives forward like a wheel. Yet, it is also the cause of all joy, life, and motion. However, if it is to be freed from this anguish and introduced into joy, it must be brought forth through "Death" <note>This refers to a spiritual or chemical transformation, a "dying" to one state to be reborn in a higher one.</note>.

40. Now, every sickness and malady is a property of death; for Mercury has ignited and inflamed itself too much in either heat or cold. By doing so, the <term>Essence</term> or flesh—which Mercury has attracted to itself through its desire within its "mother," the <term>Sulphur</term><note>original: "Sulphur"; here representing the substantial, formative energy or "container" of the life-force.</note>—is burnt. This causes "earthliness" to arise in both the water and the flesh. Just as the matter of the earth and stones (the coarseness of them) is nothing other than burnt Sulphur and water, so it is with Mercury's property: the <term>Sal Niter</term><note>original: "Sal Niter"; a term for a volatile, explosive, or energetic salt-like force (saltpeter) that Böhme associates with the flash of life.</note> in the <term>Flagrat</term><note>original: "Flagrat"; a sudden flash, outburst, or energetic explosion.</note> of the Mercurial Wheel—from which many kinds of salts arise—is burnt (or too vehemently inflamed), resulting in a foul stench and an evil taste.

41. Otherwise, if Mercury operated so effectively within the "Oil of Sulphur" that it could be brought through the "Death of the Impression" <note>The "Impression" is the contracting, hardening force of nature. To move through its "death" is to reach a state of spiritual sublimation.</note> away from the extremes of heat and cold, then the Earth would be in Paradise again. The "Joy-Desire" would spring forth (or bloom afresh) through the anguish of the cold's contraction. This is why God laid a curse upon the Earth: the Mercurial Wheel was deprived of its "Good"—that is, the Love-Desire which arises in eternal liberty and manifests itself through this Mercurial Wheel via cold and heat, proceeding through the fire to create the shining of the Light. The curse brought into the world was the withdrawing of this Love-Desire.

42. Now this Mercury, being a life within the Sulphur of its mother, exists under the curse—in the anguish of heat and cold. In its "Flagrat" or <term>Sal-nitral Walm</term><note>original: "Sal-nitral Walm"; a boiling or bubbling surge of energetic salt-properties.</note>, it continually creates salts according to the property it holds in each place and how it is ignited in each body. These salts are simply the "taste" found within the seven properties of nature.

43. Now, if Mercury is too vehemently ignited in the cold, it creates a cold, hard, contracting salt within the Sal-nitral flash of its mother (Sulphur). From this, melancholy, darkness, and sadness arise in the life of the Sulphur. Observe that whatever salt is in a thing, a corresponding luster and vital shining from the fire is also there. But if Mercury is ignited in immoderate heat, it burns up the cold essence and creates raging pains and achings according to the "Impression" and the property of the "Sting." From this, great heat and inflammation arise in the Sulphur; it dries up and consumes the water so that the Hunger or Sting of the Desire has no food to satisfy its wrathful hunger. Consequently, it rages and tears at the salt—as is the nature of poison—causing painful distemper in the flesh.

45. But if Mercury obtains "Likeness" <note>A state of balance or harmony.</note> again in its property, as it stands in the center of its mother (the Sulphur)—meaning, as she generated him in the beginning when he first came forth to natural life in the <term>Tinctures</term><note>original: "Tinctures"; the spiritual qualities or "dyes" of the soul and body.</note> of both man and woman (specifically in the child where life first ignited)—then he is freed from all anguish. He enters again into the balanced likeness of heat and cold. Although conflict arises in many even from the womb, the true combat is only raised up after the beginning of life. At the start, life enters into its highest joy, for the "Gates of the Three Principles" are opened in perfect harmony; however, the struggle for conquest between darkness and light soon begins.

46. <margin>* Enraged.</margin> We must now consider what should be done to Mercury if it becomes "enkindled" (inflamed or enraged) in either heat or cold, thereby causing sickness and pain. It would be very good if men possessed the right cure; but alas, it remains hidden and covered <margin>* Because of their bestial, lustful excess or disorder.</margin> because of the curse on the Earth and the abominations and sins of men. People awaken this poison in Mercury through their immoderate * bestiality <note>In this context, "bestiality" refers to behaving like a beast—driven by irrational lust, greed, or lack of spiritual restraint.</note>.

47. Yet the poor captive <note>referring to the human soul or body imprisoned by illness or the fall</note> has need of deliverance. Although humanity does not possess the high "Universal" remedy—which reaches the very center of being and restores the Wheel of Life to its original state—we must still take fruits from the Earth’s mercurial seething <note>original: "Walm"; the bubbling, energetic life-force within the earth</note> for that purpose, since the body has also become earthly. A person must match like with like—one salt with another—depending on how the inflammation manifests in the body’s Salt. For observe: whichever property the Sulfur <note>original: "Brimstone"</note> is ignited in—whether in heat or cold, in melancholy or epilepsy <note>original: "falling Sickness"</note>, and whether the Sulfur is burnt and putrefied or still fresh and burning—a corresponding herb or Sulfur is required for the cure. This is done so the heat or cold is not shocked in the saltpeter <note>original: "Salniter"</note> where the Salt arises by some foreign force entering it, which would generate a dead <note>original: "mort"</note> salt and further expose the "house of sadness" <note>the state of disease or misery</note>. However, an herb in its wild, natural state as it grows from the seething of the earth is not powerful enough. It cannot master the root of the ignited Mercury within the Sulfur; instead, it may only further inflame that specific condition.

48. Whatever you wish to happen to the body must first happen to the medicine that shall cure the body. To cure a "foul" sickness, one requires a "foul" Sulfur; the same logic applies to cold or hot illnesses. You must identify the degree of fire or cold in which the Mercury is ignited, and which of the seven properties of nature it belongs to—that is, which of the seven <term>Salts</term> <note>In Boehme’s alchemy, the "seven salts" refer to the seven planetary properties or qualities of nature.</note> is inflamed. A matching salt belongs to the cure. For sickness is nothing more than a "hunger," and this hunger desires nothing but its own likeness. The root of life is that property which stood in joy at its beginning; sickness is merely its immoderate burning, which breaks and divides the natural balance <note>original: "Order [or Temperature]"</note>. Thus, the root hungers for its likeness, but the inflammation has consumed it. Because the inflammation is stronger than the root, the hunger of the inflammation must be satisfied; medicine that matches the nature of the inflammation itself must be administered to it.

49. Consider how God cured us with His love and restored the soul’s salvation when we had ignited it in the poisonous "Mercury" of His anger. In the same way, this "likeness" <note>the medicinal substance</note> must first be cured and refined <note>original: "circulated"</note> in the mercurial wheel to be freed from extreme heat and cold. These qualities are not actually removed—which would be impossible and useless—but are instead brought into their highest "joy" <note>their most refined, beneficial state</note>. Then, the medicine will produce a similar property within the body's Mercury, Sulfur, and Salt. The root of life will revive itself through this, raising its original desire so that the hunger of the sickness vanishes as the inflammation subsides.

50. Now, the physician must know how to handle these medicines so he does not agitate them or force them into a different property. In their own nature, they are just like a human life. He must ensure they remain in their proper "degree," just as they were originally brought forth by their "Mother" <note>Nature or the source of the plant/mineral</note>. Nothing can rise higher than its own original hidden center. If a substance is forced to a higher degree, it assumes a different property and loses its true, proper virtue in exchange for an improper one. While this can be done, the substance loses its natural right <note>its inherent balanced state</note> wherein it exists in joy, and it becomes unable to perform its proper healing operation on its counterpart in the body.

51. Therefore, nothing is better than to let everything remain in its innate, genuine virtue. Only its "wrath" <note>the harsh or toxic aspect</note> must be changed into its own "joy," so that its good qualities may gain dominance. Then, in its likeness, it is powerful enough to treat all sicknesses without needing any other mixtures. The original root of life desires no complexity, only its own likeness, so that it may stand, live, and burn in its own power and property.

52. The power of the Most High has given all things a fixed perfection, each according to its property. All was "very good," as Moses says, but with the...

By the curse, the *Turba* <note>original: *Turba*, referring to the spirit of turmoil, disruption, or "the disturber" in nature</note> is introduced, so that the properties exist in the strife of *Mercury*. Yet in each property—in every herb, in whatever exists, or whatever grows or arises out of the boiling <margin>*Boiling*.</margin> <note>original: *Walm*</note> of the four elements—there is a hidden stability. For all things that are in the four elements originally sprang forth out of the eternal element, in which there is no strife, neither heat nor cold. Has God given us the power to become his children and to rule over the world? Why then not over the curse of the earth? Let no one consider it impossible; it requires only a divine understanding and knowledge. This shall blossom in the *Time of the Lily* <note>Böhme’s term for a future age of spiritual enlightenment and peace</note>, and not in *Babel* <note>The "city of confusion," representing false religious systems and worldly wisdom</note>, for whom we have not written.

## The Fourteenth Chapter.

### Concerning the *Wheel* of *Sulphur*, *Mercury*, and *Salt*; the *Generation* of *Good* and *Evil*; showing how one is changed into the other, and how one manifests its property in the other, and yet both remain in the first creation in the wonder of **GOD** for his own manifestation and glory.

<margin>Or *what it is*.</margin>
1. This is an open gate to the preceding description. Everyone says, "Show me the way to the *manifestation of the good*." Listen and observe well, dear *Reason*; you must be the way yourself. The understanding must be born in you; otherwise, I cannot show it to you. You must enter into it yourself so that the understanding of the work in its practical art—which is not my focus here—may be opened to you. I write only in the spirit of contemplation, explaining how the generation of good and evil occurs, and opening the fountain. He whom God has appointed for the task shall draw the water; here, I will only describe the wheel of life as it is in itself.

2. When I speak of *Sulphur*, *Mercury*, and *Salt*, I am speaking of one single thing, whether it is spiritual or physical. All created things are that one thing, but the properties in the generation of this single thing create differences [or provide various gradual distinctions]. For when I name a man, or a lion, bear, wolf, hare, or any other beast—or even a root, herb, tree, or whatever may be named—it is the same single thing.

3. Everything that is physical is the same being: the herbs and trees, as well as the animals, but each thing differs according to its first beginning. Just as the property in the *Verbum Fiat* <note>Latin: "The Word: Let it be done," referring to the creative command of God</note> has imprinted itself into each thing, so is that kind in its reproduction. All things exist in the seed and procreation, and there is nothing that does not have a stability in it—whether it is hidden or manifest—for all things shall stand for the glory of God.

<summary>Böhme explains that the harmonious "Paradise" state remains hidden within the turbulent natural world and can be recovered through divine understanding. He introduces the triad of Sulphur, Mercury, and Salt as the universal foundation of all life, reflecting God's creative word.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Chapter 14 of Signatura Rerum, moving from the discussion of the "Signature of all things" toward a deeper exploration of the "Mother" or the source of all nature and its seven properties.</meta>

# Signatura Rerum: Chapter 14

4. Whatever has risen from the eternal fixity, such as angels and the souls of human beings, remains indestructible in its fixed being. But whatever has risen in an unfixed being—that is, within the movement of time—enters again into the first motion from which it originated. It remains only as a map of the form it had here, like a picture or an image in a mirror without life. This is how it existed from eternity before the beginning of this world, which the Most High introduced into an image—into a comprehensible, natural life in time—so that His great wonders of wisdom could be seen in a created being, as we clearly see.

5. Now we must consider the only Mother <note>Boehme uses "Mother" to refer to the divine matrix or the foundational force of Nature.</note> and her properties. From her, the infinite variety of things arises and has always risen. We must see how she generates life and death, evil and good, and how all things may be brought back into their first essence <note>original: "Ens"</note>—that is, back to the place where they originally arose. In this process, death—or the act of dying—is the greatest mystery.

6. For nothing that has left its first order—as the Mother brought it forth—can go back and enter its root with its acquired order, unless it dies to that acquired order within its Mother. Only then is it once again at the end and in the place from which it was created. Thus, it stands again in the *Verbum Fiat* <note>Latin: "Let it be done"—the creative Word of God mentioned in Genesis.</note>, within the boundary of its order in the expressed Word. It may then enter again into what it was in the beginning before it became physical. There it is "good," for it stands once more in the source from which it proceeded.

7. Now, therefore, let us consider the beginnings of all things. We cannot say that this world was made out of something pre-existing. It was purely and simply a desire arising out of the free <term>Lubet</term> <note>From the Latin "libitum," meaning pleasure or inclination. In Boehme's work, it refers to the Divine Will's innate longing to manifest itself.</note>, so that the Abyss <note>The "Unground" or the bottomless, infinite void of the Godhead.</note>—the highest Good or Being, the Eternal Will—might see itself in that delight as if in a mirror. Therefore, the Eternal Will conceived this delight and turned it into a desire. This desire impressed, shaped, and embodied itself into both a body and a spirit according to the properties of that impression. As this impression organized itself into various forms, the possibilities (or powers) arose within it as "Nature."

<margin>Mirror.</margin>
8. This impression is the only mother of the manifestation of the mystery, and it is called Nature and Essence. It makes manifest what has existed from eternity in the Eternal Will. Yet we should understand that there was an eternal nature within the Eternal Will, like an eternal mind within the will. However, it was only a spirit in the will; the essence of its power was not made manifest except in the looking-glass of the will. This mirror is the Eternal Wisdom, in which all things in this world were known in two centers: first, according to fire and light, and then according to darkness and essence. All of these came into a manifest mystery through the movement of the Eternal Will and the desire within that will, thus introducing themselves into a manifest possibility.

<margin>Or shapes.</margin>
9. This is now the essence expressed or made manifest out of eternity into time. It consists of the previously mentioned forms of <term>Sulphur</term>, <term>Mercury</term>, and <term>Salt</term> <note>In alchemy, these represent the "tria prima" or three primary principles: expansion (Sulphur), contraction/flow (Mercury), and the solidifying result (Salt).</note>, where one is not divided or separated from the others. It is one eternal essence and shapes itself into the properties of desire according to the possibilities of manifestation. We must understand that one property does not, and cannot, exist without the others; they are altogether the same single possibility. Now we will speak of their differences—specifically, how this single possibility introduces itself into good and evil, or into quiet peace and constant restlessness.

<margin>Or Attraction.</margin>
10. We find seven special properties in nature by which this only Mother works all things. These are: First, the **Desire**, which is astringent, cold, hard, and dark. Second, the **Bitter**, which is the "sting" of the astringent, hard enclosure; this is the cause of all motion and life. Third, the **Anguish**, caused by the raging in...

# Signatura Rerum: Chapter 14

In the fourth form <note>original: "Form"; Boehme uses "Forms" to describe the seven fundamental properties of nature</note>, the coarseness <note>original: "Grossness"</note> dies away, and it is received again in the fifth form, namely in the love-desire. Again, it proceeds forth in its own property in the love-desire and creates the sixth form, namely the sound, voice, or tone out of the fire and water.

18. Now this tone or sound, which is called *Mercury*, arises in the first form—the compression <note>original: "Impression"</note>—by reason of the will and attractive desire. For the attraction creates the motions and the stinging <note>original: "Compunction"</note> in the hardness, which we distinguish and call the second form; however, it is a son of the first, and exists within the first.

<margin>Or the first property.</margin>
<margin>Or the sting in the hardness, namely the hardness itself.</margin>

19. This second form or property is the raging, stinging, and bitter pain. For the first is contracting <note>original: "astringent"</note> and the second is drawing—namely, the desire into a substance <note>original: "Essence"</note>. This same substance is the <gloss>property of the first</gloss>, and the attraction creates within it the second property: a bitter stinging which the hardness cannot endure. For the hardness would prefer to be still, and therefore it compresses itself more vehemently to withhold the sting, yet the sting only grows greater because of it. Now the hardness, namely the astringency, draws inwards, and the sting <gloss>from the hardness upwards</gloss>. From this arises the first enmity and opposition; for the two forms, which are actually only one, make themselves their own enemies. And yet, if this did not happen, there would be no substance, neither body nor spirit, nor any manifestation of the eternity of the abyss <note>original: "Abyss"; the infinite void or groundless "Ungrund" of God</note>.

<margin>Understand the Mother of Sulphur.</margin>

20. But now, seeing that the bitter sting cannot ascend and the hardness also cannot hold or enclose it, they fall into a turning or breaking through like a wheel, which runs into itself as a terrifying substance where both properties are known only as one. Yet each remains in itself unaltered, and they produce the third property between them: the great anguish. Out of this anguish, the *will* (meaning the fixed will toward nature) desires to go forth again into liberty—that is, into the "nothing," into eternal rest. For here it has found itself and manifested itself, and yet there is no separating or departing. This anxious form is the mother of *Sulphur*, for the sting makes <gloss>it painful</gloss> and the hardness compresses it, so that it is like a dying source, and yet it is the true origin of life.

21. It has two properties within itself: according to the compression or desire, it is dark and hard; and according to the desire of the will, which wants to be free from the anguish and enter again into liberty, it is spiritual and light. The sting breaks into pieces its conceived substance <note>original: "Essence"</note> which the contracting desire holds within itself, so that its substance is hard and split <note>original: "spalt"</note>, darting wholly like a flash of lightning from the darkness and from the desire of the light—meaning, toward liberty.

<margin>First Matter <note>original: "Prima Materia"</note>.</margin>

22. Now these three forms are in one substance as a raging spirit. The desire compresses these properties so that a substance is made according to their property, based on the first origin: the contracting, dark desire. This is an earthly substance, out of which the Earth was made in the beginning of the "great motion." According to the bitter, raging spirit, there is an instigation in the substance—namely, a poison—which also imprints itself in the substance, which is why the earthliness is so completely loathsome and bitter. The third form, the anguish, provides a fiery property to it. And yet, at this stage, there cannot yet be a physical substance; it is only a spiritual substance and the <gloss>mother to the substance</gloss>.

23. The fourth form in this substance is the fire. One part of its origin comes from the dark, hard compression—from the hardness and the raging sting in the anguish—which is the cold black fire and the pain of the great anguish. The other part takes its origin in the spirit of the will toward nature, which goes back out of this hard, dark coldness into itself—namely, into liberty, without the nature of the harsh motion. This enkindles liberty—the eternal longing <note>original: "Lubet"; the divine inclination or delight</note> for the desire of nature—with its sharpness, which it has conceived in the compression. Through this, it becomes a moving and stirring luster <note>original: "Luster"; a shining or radiance</note>. For liberty is neither dark nor light, but by reason...

# Chap. 14.

Regarding the motion, it is light; for its <term>lubet</term> <note>original: "lubet"; Boehme’s term for a divine inclination, delight, or longing within the will</note> brings itself into the desire for light so that it may be manifest in light and luster. Yet it cannot happen except through darkness, so that the light might be known and made manifest, and the Eternal Mind might find and manifest itself. For a Will is only one thing and essence, but through multiplicity its form is made manifest—showing that it is infinite and a pure wonder. We speak of this with a child's tongue, being only like a small spark out of these great, infinite wonders.

24. Now understand us this way: Liberty exists and stands within the darkness <margin>Or opposite to the dark desire, or dark impression, which follows the desire for light.</margin>. Along with the Eternal Will, it reaches toward the darkness, while the darkness reaches after the light of Liberty but cannot attain it. For darkness encloses itself within its own desire and becomes darkness within itself. Out of both of these—that is, out of the dark impression and out of the desire of Liberty toward that impression—there is a twinkling or darting flash within the impression, which is the origin of the fire. For Liberty shines into the impression, but the impression, in its anguish, grasps it into itself, and so it appears as a flash. But because Liberty is incomprehensible and like a "nothing"—and, moreover, exists outside and before the impression and is <term>abyssal</term> <margin>Or without any ground.</margin> <note>original: "abyssal"; referring to the "Ungrund," Boehme's concept of the "groundless" or bottomless nature of the divine before creation</note>—the impression cannot conceive or hold it. Instead, the impression gives itself into Liberty, and Liberty devours its dark property and essence, ruling within the darkness with an assumed mobility that remains ungraspable to the darkness.

25. Thus, understand us correctly: there is a devouring within the fire. The sharpness of the fire comes from the harsh impression of coldness and bitterness, which comes from anguish; and the devouring comes from Liberty, which, according to its own property, turns "something" back into "nothing" again.

26. And understand us very precisely: Liberty does not wish to be a "nothing." Therefore, the <term>lubet</term> of Liberty introduces itself into nature and essence so that it might be manifest in power, wonder, and being. Through the sharpness of the cold and dark impression, it also takes on properties so that it might manifest the power of Liberty. For it consumes the dark essence in the fire and proceeds out of the fire—out of the anguish of the impression—carrying spiritual properties into the light. As you can see, the outward light shines out of the fire in this way, yet it does not contain the source or pain of the fire within itself, but only its property. The light reveals the properties of the darkness, but only within itself; the darkness remains dark in itself, and the light continues to be light in itself.

27. Liberty (which is called God) is the cause of the light, and the impression of desire is the cause of the darkness and the painful <term>source</term> <note>original: "source"; in Boehme’s German, "Qual," which carries the dual meaning of a "wellspring" (Quelle) and "torment" (Qual)</note>. Now, herein understand two eternal beginnings—that is, two principles: one in the Liberty within the light, the other in the impression within the pain and source of the darkness, each dwelling within itself.

28. And understand us further concerning their unfolding essence and will, and how nature is introduced into seven properties. We do not speak of a "beginning," for there is no beginning in eternity. Rather, the eternal generation continues from eternity to eternity within itself. This same eternal generation—according to the property of eternity and through its own desire and motion—has introduced itself into time along with this visible world. This world is a likeness of the Eternal Spirit, a creaturely being that serves as a type or platform of the Eternal Being. We will speak of this later and show what a "creature" is—namely, a likeness of the operation of eternity—and how it also contains this same eternal working within its temporal self.

29. Now, regarding the fire, understand us this way: fire is the principle of every life. To the darkness, it gives essence and a <term>source</term>; otherwise, there would be no sensibility in the darkness, nor any spirit, but only pure hardness—a hard, sharp, bitter, galling sting, as it truly is in the eternal darkness. But so far as the hot fire may be <term>obtained</term> <margin>Or reached.</margin>...

36. Now, understand us correctly; we do not mean a beginning of the Deity itself, but the *manifestation* of the Deity. The Deity is known and manifested here as a Trinity. The Deity is the eternal liberty without any nature—namely, the eternal abyss <note>original: "Abyss"; Böhme uses this to mean the "groundless" or the infinite void before creation.</note>. This is the outgoing power in the flame of love; we speak only of parts of the Universal Whole as it relates to a creature.

38. The Deity is entirely everywhere, all in all; but He is only called "God" according to the light of love and the proceeding spirit of joy. However, according to the dark impression, He is called God’s anger and the dark world; and according to the eternal fire-spirit, He is called a consuming fire.

39. We only intend to give you an understanding of the Being of all beings, whose origin in itself is only one eternal essence. But through its own manifestation, it comes into many beings for its own honor and glory. Now we will show you what the creature’s life and dominion is in this all-essential Being.

<margin>Or genuine property.</margin>
40. Therefore, understand correctly what we mean by these three words: *Sulphur*, *Mercury*, and *Sal* <note>In Böhme’s alchemy, these represent the three fundamental principles of existence: Sulphur (the soul/fire), Mercury (the spirit/motion), and Sal (the body/matter).</note>. In eternity, all is spirit; but when God moved Himself within the eternal nature—in which His own manifestation consists—He produced a palpable and manifest essence out of the spiritual essence. He introduced it into a creaturely being according to the eternal properties, which also consists of spirit and essence, according to the law of eternity.

41. And now I will speak of the outward kingdom—namely, of the third principle or beginning. For in this world, there is also light and darkness within each other, just as in eternity. God has given this world a sun as a "nature-god" of the outward powers, but He rules within it as Lord. The outward kingdom is only His prepared work, which He rules and creates with its counterpart <note>original: "Assimilate"</note>, just as a master performs his work with a tool.

42. *Sulphur* is the first mother of the creatures in the outward world—that is, in the mystery of the great God’s manifestation. It arises out of darkness, fire, and light. On one hand, according to the dark impression, it is restrictive, bitter, and anxious. On the other hand, toward the Deity and as an image of the Deity, it is fire, light, and water. In the fire, it separates itself into two forms: through "mortification" <note>original: "Mortification"; the alchemical process of transformation through symbolic death.</note> it becomes water, and according to the life, it becomes oil. In this oil, the true life of all the creatures of the outward world consists.

43. *Mercury* is the wheel of motion within the *Sulphur*. On one hand, according to the dark impression, it is the stinging rage and the great restlessness. It also separates itself in the fire within its mother (the Sulphur) into two properties—namely, into a twofold water. For in the "killing" of the fire, everything is turned to water. For as the spirit's property is, so also is its water; and even so it is in the fire-flagrat <term>flagrat</term> <note>Boehme uses "flagrat" to describe a sudden, explosive burst or flash that marks a transformation between states of being.</note>.

45. Furthermore, understand us regarding the fiery flagrat concerning the <term>salniter</term> <note>original: Salniter; saltpeter or niter, which Boehme views as a potent, explosive "universal salt" that acts as a creative or destructive force.</note>, from which the many salts and powers arise. For all the properties of the spirit have become corporeal in the great motion of the "essence of all essences" and entered into a visible and comprehensible being. This flagrat is caused by the enkindling of the fire; and in the mortification <note>original: mortification; the alchemical process of "dying" or the breaking down of a substance's outer form to release its inner nature.</note> of the fire, it draws into itself from the water's origin a water according to the property of the flagrat. This is more fire than water, yet its mortal essence is a water according to the property of the flagrat. It is the gathering of all properties; it brings forth in its comprehension—that is, in the fiery flagrat—all properties within itself. It seizes the property of the light in its powers, and also the property of the dark impression in its powers, and makes all things fiery: one part according to the coldness, and one part according to the heat, but for the most part according to the endless <term>mercury</term>, which is the life of all essences in both evil and good, in light and darkness.

46. This <term>salniter</term> is the mother of all salts in vegetables and animals—that is, in herbs, trees, and every thing. He is the first root in all things that give a taste and smell, according to each thing's property. In the good (which grow in the love-desire in the oil of brimstone <note>original: brimstone; sulfur, representing the passionate or energetic principle.</note>), he is good, powerful, and pleasant; and in the evil, he is evil in the anguish of brimstone. And in the darkness, he is the eternal horror and despair, continually desiring in the flagrat to rise above the gates in the fire, from which arises the will of all devils and of all pride—to ascend above the humility of the love-desire. In the fire is the trial of his essence, as we see how he clashes and consumes himself in the flash like a sudden thought.

47. For its essence does not arise in the essence of eternity, nor can it inherit it, but rather in the enkindling of the temporal fire; yet it is perceived in the Eternal Spirit because of the elevation of joy. But according to the essence of mortification—that is, according to the salt of the fire—it subsists in the fire. For this property arises out of the first desire—that is, in the essence of the first impression—which property the philosophers call <term>saturn</term> <note>Saturn is associated with lead, weight, contraction, and the beginning of the alchemical process.</note>. Therefore, the salt is manifold. All sharpness in the taste is salt; the good taste arises out of the oily <note>original: oleous</note> salt, as does the smell, which is the outgoing spirit in which the <term>tincture</term> <note>original: Tincture; the spiritual soul or inner "dye" of a substance that gives it its virtues and color.</note> appears as a luster or beautiful complexion of colors.

48. Thus, understand us correctly: the <term>salniter</term> in the fire-flagrat is the separation of the properties, where death and life separate themselves. This means the life which enters with the love-desire into an essence and dominion; and then the life which—in the flagrat of death, according to the property of the cold—sinks down in the mortification of the flagrat as an impotency <note>original: impotency; a state of powerlessness or lack of life-force.</note> and provides weight. According to its subtlety, it produces water; according to the grossness of its harshness, it produces earth; and according to sulfur and <term>mercury</term>, it produces sand and stones. According to the subtlety in sulfur and <term>mercury</term>—understand this according to the water of the same—it makes flesh. According to the anxious darkness, it makes a smoke or rust; but according to the oily property—that is, according to the love-desire—it makes a sweet spiritual essence; and according to the spirit, a pleasant smell; and according to the moving of the fire and light, it makes the [one] element.

<summary>Boehme explains the alchemical and spiritual origins of matter through the "fire-flagrat," a transformative burst where "salniter" (saltpeter) separates into various physical and spiritual properties. He details how different elements like salt, water, and earth arise from the interplay of light, darkness, and mercury.</summary>

...and from the luster in the flash of fire, combined with the appearance of light, comes the precious tincture <note>original: "Tincture"; in alchemy, a spiritualized essence or "dye" that transforms matter</note>. This tincture colors all oily salts, giving rise to pleasant tastes and smells.

<margin>Seething.</margin>
49. The "salnitral flash" <note>original: "Salnitral Flagrat"; a term referring to the sudden ignition or energetic burst of saltpeter, used by Boehme to describe a spiritual/chemical transition</note> is the seething <note>original: "Sude"; a boiling or bubbling up</note> within the essence. From this, growth and budding <note>original: "pullulation"</note> arise, so that there is a process of growing within the structure of that essence. The salt acts as the preservation or support of the essence, allowing a thing to exist as a body or a tangible form. It holds the *sulfur* and *mercury* together; otherwise, they would separate from each other during the fire-flash.

<margin>A seething,</margin>
50. All things consist of *sulfur*, *mercury*, and *salt*. Within the salnitral flash, the Element <note>The "one Element" or quintessence from which the four physical elements originate</note> separates itself into four properties: *fire*, *air*, *water*, and *earth*. In itself, the Element is none of these, but is only a moving and gentle <gloss>bubbling</gloss>—not like the wind, but like the movement of the will within the body, which is the cause of life in the essence. For just as the eternal Spirit of God proceeds from the Father (who is a Spirit from the fire and light and is the motion and life of eternity), so likewise the *air* proceeds forth continually out of all the properties in the salnitral flash within the fire. It arises from the anguish in the *sulfur* within the driving *mercurial* wheel as an impetuous, upward-striving motion. It is a "son" of all the properties and is also their life. The fire of all the forms provides the air and also receives it back again for its own life. The water is its body, where it creates the seething in the saltpeter, and the earth is its power, where it kindles its strength and fire-soul.

51. There is only one single Element, and it unfolds itself into four parts during the salnitral flash. With its ignition, it produces a consuming fire out of the darkness and its essence. In the "flash of dying" <note>the transition where the "cold" and "dark" qualities are transformed</note>—where cold and darkness cease—it divides itself into essences: according to its subtlety into water, and according to its coarseness into earth. Then, according to the motion of the flash's bubbling, it becomes air. Air most closely resembles the [one] Element, but it is not entirely the same essence; for the one Element is neither hot nor cold, nor is it forceful or compulsive, but moves gently.

## *Of the Desire of the Properties.*

52. **Every** property maintains its own desire; for a property is nothing more than a hunger, and that hunger forms itself into an essence like itself. In the salnitral seething, it sends such a spirit into the four elements; for the origin of the seething is in the one Element, from which the four elements proceed during this flash.

<margin>As to its life in the four elements; but every creature does not have the true life of the Element, but only an inward motion.</margin>
53. Each body exists <gloss>within its life in the four elements; but every creature does not have the true life of the one Element, but only an inward motion</gloss> within the inward motion of the Element, and within the growth and life of the four *elements*. However, not every creature possesses the true life of the Element—only the high spirits, such as angels and human souls, which exist in the first principle <note>the realm of eternal spirit</note>. In them, the Element can be stirred. In the life of the third principle <note>the physical, visible world</note>, it stands still and acts as the "hand of God," where He holds and governs the four elements as an expression or instrument with which He works and builds.

54. Now, every property of *Nature*, driven by its hunger, takes its food from the four *elements*. As the hunger is, so it takes a property from the *elements*; for the four *elements* are the body of these properties, and each spirit feeds on its own body.

55. First, there are the sulfurous properties according to the first and second impressions: namely, according to the dark, restrictive <note>original: "astringent"</note>, and anxious impression; and then according to the impression of love in the light—that is, according to both evil and good.

56. The dark hunger desires an essence that matches its property—namely, earthly things and everything that resembles the earth. The bitter hunger desires bitter raging, stinging, and pain; it absorbs such an essence (like a source of poison) from the elements. The hunger of anguish desires a state of anxiety, namely the anguish found in the brimstone <note>sulfur</note>. Likewise, the melancholy temperament takes the desire for death and continual sadness; and

The Fire-Flash <note>A sudden spiritual or physical ignition of energy.</note> absorbs anger, aspiration, ambition, and pride—a desire to destroy all and make everything subject to itself. it is a desire to dominate in and above everything, to consume all, and to be unique. It draws bitterness from the source of the flash into envy and hatred, and it draws harshness <note>original: "Astringency"</note> into greed, and the fire itself into anger and indignation.

<margin>Anger.</margin>
57. Here is the true desire of God's anger and of all devils, and of everything that is against God and love. This hunger draws such an essence into the self, as can be recognized and examined in living creatures and also in herbs.

<margin>Spirit.</margin>
58. Now, the Fire-Flash is the end of the first desire—that is, the dark nature—and in the fire, the death of the first hunger and will begins. The fire consumes all the coarseness <note>original: "Grossness"</note> of the first forms and casts them into death. Here is the separation of both wills: one enters back into the property of death and is a will living within the dark desire. This is what the devils have done; they wanted to dominate within the Fire-Flash in the salnitral seething <note>original: "Salnitral Sude"; a term for the boiling or explosive energy of saltpeter, used here as a metaphor for spiritual agitation.</note> over time and eternity, but they were driven back by the Spirit of God and spat out of the desire for love as an abomination. This is also what happens to the wicked soul of man, which is followed by the process of "Election" <note>The theological concept of God's choice in salvation.</note>. Here is the aim or scope of the election of grace of which the Scripture speaks: that God knows his own. Here, the eternal delight <term>Lubet</term> <note>original: "Lubet"; from the German *Lust*, referring to God's pure, free inclination or joyous will.</note> of God's liberty captures the will-spirit that arose in the dark center and brings it through the death in the fire and into the "Element" <note>The pure, heavenly substance.</note>.

59. In the salnitral flash <note>original: "Salnitral Flagrat"</note>, the possibility lies both backward and forward. If the will of the desire goes backward, it belongs to the kingdom of this world (the earthly) and to the kingdom of the eternal world in God's anger; it cannot see God unless it is converted and enters into the death in the fire, dying wholly to its self-interest. It must enter into the resignation of the eternal will through the salnitral flash and into the Element—that is, into the heavenly essence and physicality—so that its hunger may eat of the pure Element. Then it has no other desire, for in the fire it has died to the harsh, dark hunger which is evil. Thus, from the death in the fire, the light arises, for here liberty is ignited, becoming its own hunger and desire. This is now a love-desire and a love-hunger.

60. In the outward world, this is the light of the sun within the four elements, and it is the animal love-desire—namely, for the sulfurous <note>original: "Sulphurean"</note> body and essence, from which mating and multiplication arise (the vegetative life). From the mercury <note>The active, communicative principle in alchemy.</note> in the saltpeter <note>original: "Salniter"</note> (in which the sensible life exists), the astral influence <note>original: "Astrum"</note> provides reason to the animals based on the properties of the saltpeter.

<margin>The Word "Let it be" in the, etc.</margin>
<margin>Or seethe.</margin>
61. For the entire astral realm is nothing else but a saltpeter within the Word "Let it be" <note>original: "Verbum Fiat"; the creative command of God.</note>, in the motion of the Being of all beings in the fiery flash. It is contained within the properties of the salts, where all the powers of the Element stand as an external birth. These powers continually boil in the four elements like a salnitral salt, introducing their properties through their desire in the four elements into the essence of bodies, as can be seen in trees, herbs, grass, and all growing things.

62. Therefore, understand us further concerning the second center, which is revealed in the dying of the fire into the light. Through this, the abyss of God's liberty introduces itself into the foundation <note>original: "Byss"</note> of nature—both within the inward world in the Kingdom of Heaven in eternity, and also within the outward kingdom in time.

63. Now, all of this also possesses the properties of desire and originates from the first principle (the first center), yet there is not yet a true death in the fire. Only the dark essence dies, and the will-spirit goes forth with the eternal will back toward nature, out of the fiery death and into the light. It is merely a transformation <note>original: "Transmutation"</note> of the spirit, so that a hunger arises out of liberty, and this hunger is a love-desire. As for the soul of man, it draws essence from the Element of God—that is, in the divine saltpeter, it takes the divine salts or powers into itself. And as for the outward world's...

The Desire draws the Oil out of the Sulphur into itself; in this Oil, the outward life burns. It is the same in plants, metals, and all other things.

64. The Sun performs the external transformation <note>original: "Transmutation"</note>, and the divine Light within the soul’s essential nature <note>original: "Property"</note> performs the internal transformation. According to the level or degree in which each thing stands, its "hunger" reaches for a specific quality. Those things which exist in Time receive their qualities from Time, and those in Eternity likewise receive theirs from Eternity. The hunger that proceeds from Eternity eats of Eternity, and that which is of Time eats of Time. The true life of all creatures eats of the spiritual Mercury <note>In Boehme’s alchemy, *Mercury* represents the spirit of motion and the "Word" through which life is expressed</note>—that is, of the "sixth form" <note>Boehme describes seven forms or properties of Nature; the sixth is the "Sound" or "Speech" where the spirit becomes audible and expressive</note>, where all Salts are essentially found. The Spirit eats of the five senses, for they are the Spirit’s physical form; and the body—that is, the plant-like life—eats of the essence of the Sulphur and Salt <note>Sulphur represents the "soul" or inner fire, and Salt represents the physical "body" or structure</note>. For Christ says in a similar way:
> *Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word which proceeds out of the mouth of God.*

65. Now, the sixth form of Nature is the expressed spiritual Word, and the speaking Word within it is the Eternal Word. In its first impression within the Darkness, it is the Word of God's anger; and in the outward world, it is the poisonous *Mercury*—the cause of all life and movement, and of all tones and sounds. Every quality eats of its own likeness according to its level. The hunger of Time eats of Time, and the hunger of Eternity eats of Eternity—both the Spirit of *Mercury* and the Spirit of *Sulphur*. Yet, these are not two separate spirits, but only two properties of the same thing. Anything that originates from only one principle, such as the creatures of the outward world, has only one region of existence, though it has a two-fold inclination toward both good and evil. But whatever originates from two principles, like Man, has a two-fold source of food and dominion: from the dark center and from the outward center. However, if a person dies to his "Self-hood" <note>the ego or self-centered will</note> and brings his hunger into God's Kingdom, then he may eat of the divine *Mercury*—namely, of the five divine senses with the soul, and of the Element within the divine Essence. Yet, the outward man does not grasp the divine Essence physically in this lifetime, but only through the imagination <note>original: *Imaginatio*; the creative power of the mind to shape spiritual reality</note>, where the inward body penetrates the outward. It is like the Sun shining through water: the water remains water, yet it is filled with light. This is where our *Fall in Adam* lies.

66. The pure Element once completely penetrated the four physical elements, and they were entirely one in Man. But through the Curse, the pure Element separated from the soul, so that the poor soul now lives only in the "vessel" of the four physical elements <note>the material body</note>, unless it enters again into the death of its earthly will and springs forth once more in the pure Element through divine desire.

<margin>Nausea, Abomination.</margin>
67. Thus, the outward body is also under the Curse and eats from the properties of the cursed earth—specifically, from the earthly saltpeter <note>original: "Salniter"; Boehme uses this term to describe a volatile, energetic mineral force that he believed drove growth and decay</note>. Here, one hunger of the earthly properties continually opposes another, for the Curse is a loathsome abomination in all "Salts." This is why a constant conflict arises in the outward body; one quality's hunger catches the "abomination" <note>corruption or disharmony</note> from the other. Now, to help the body be freed from this abomination, it must take in a remedy that is "like" the abomination—the very thing that causes nausea—which has risen in the body like a "seething" or boiling. This must be introduced into the "dying of the fire" and brought out into the "Love-Desire" to be freed from the Curse of vanity. This is achieved in no other way than by the true life dying to its dark vanity.

68. The abomination of the outward life arises from a property of the Salt which is contrary to the "Oil of Life." Thus, the abomination immediately ignites itself in the four elements and begins to boil in the saltpeter like an alien life. This "strange life" eventually darkens and destroys the first true life if it is not resisted. It can have no better help than a remedy that is similar to <note>original: "the Assimulate of"</note> the introduced abomination that the life has taken into itself. Therefore, that which is done to the life to free it from the abomination must also be done to create the cure.

69. The cure itself must be freed from that same abomination, which it received in the four elements from a similar false influence <note>original: "Insinuation, Influence, or Impression"</note>. It must be brought into...

<summary>Boehme explains how all life is sustained by a "hunger" for qualities corresponding to its origin, whether temporal or eternal. He describes the human condition as a struggle between the corrupt "abomination" of the material elements and the potential for spiritual restoration through the "divine Mercury."</summary>

...the death of the four elements, and its spirit must also be infused <note>original: "tinctured"</note> in the fifth form with the *Venus* desire—that is, with a pleasant essence—so that the spiritual <term>Mercury</term> <note>In Böhme’s system, Mercury represents the volatile, moving principle of life and nature.</note> may arise in <term>Jupiter's</term> <note>Jupiter represents the quality of wisdom, justice, and calm power.</note> property. Understand this: the cure must first die to its sickness in all the four elements. It must be introduced into the putrefaction of all the four elements: in the fire, it dies to its earthliness; in the putrefaction, it dies to the water's earthliness; and in the air's putrefaction, it dies to the <term>Abominate</term> <note>original: "Abominate"; the corruption, impurity, or "curse" that causes sickness or sin.</note> and earthliness of the air. Then it must be brought into *Venus*, and from *Venus* into *Jupiter*, and then the Sun will arise in the love-desire. With this, the Abominate in the body may be resisted.

<margin>The unregenerate.</margin>
70. All other cures which are administered raw and undigested—as when one takes cold to resist heat, or heat to resist cold—are only an opposite fiery <term>Flagrat</term> <note>A sudden, violent flash or burst of energy/fire.</note>. By this, the ignited fire indeed ceases its powerful working, but the flash enters into death's anguish, and the root of the Abominate becomes a poisonous *Mercury*, unless the heat and cold are first tempered with *Venus* and *Jupiter*. If they are tempered, then it truly is an appeasing of the Abominate in the <term>Salnitral Sude</term> <note>The "seething" or boiling of saltpeter; a metaphor for the turbulent, creative energy in nature.</note>. But the root of the Abominate remains still, unless the life is strong and mightily brings forth its desire out of the Abominate. Physicians must well observe this: raw herbs do not reach the root where the Abominate has arisen in the center of the life's form. They reach only the four elements and give some easement, but the Abominate remains in the root as a hidden sickness.

71. The same is also to be understood concerning the <term>Astrum</term> <note>The "Star" or astral influence that governs the physical body's temperament.</note>, which has its "boiling" in the outward body as a distinct body within the four elements. If the cure can be freed from the Abominate of the four elements, then the *Astrum* also falls into the good part and introduces its desire into it. Thus, the body is also freed from the Abominate of the *Astrum*. For the Scripture says:
<margin>Or all creatures.</margin>
> *That the whole creation groans together with us to be freed from vanity.* <note>A reference to Romans 8:22.</note>

Now, the curse of the earth—into which the *Astrum* injects its desire—is that vanity. If it tastes a pure life within itself, it also rejoices in it and casts forth the Abominate.

<margin>Nausea or loathsomeness.</margin>
72. Every Abominate of the oily life arises from the inward *Mercury* in the inward <term>Sulphur</term> <note>Sulphur represents the "soul" or the flammable, energetic substance of a thing.</note>. For sin also takes its origin from this: that the poisonous *Mercury* (which is a cause of life) introduces itself back into "self-hood" during the fire-flash in the origin of the <term>Salniter</term>. Right there is the origin of the "poison-life."

<margin>Entire.</margin>
73. Every life that wishes to be without spot must die in its "will-spirit" to nature. It must die in the fire of the Abominate to the first impression of wrath. It must give itself forth as a resigned will through <term>Mortification</term> <note>The alchemical and spiritual process of "dying" to one's current state to reach a higher perfection.</note> in the light of love. Whether it is heavenly or earthly, it must undergo that process, or else it does not come to the highest perfection of its degree. For mankind could not be helped unless the love-center of the "love-desire" entered again into humanity and brought forth its own life—namely, the human self—through mortification into itself. This is an exact model or resemblance: whatever is to be freed from the Abominate (the curse) must die to the four elements within that Abominate and bring forth its higher state through the mortification of the fire in the light.

74. Thus it is also with the *Salnitral Sude* in the earth, from which metals, good herbs, and trees grow. Each property desires its own likeness. If it can reach its likeness in *Sulphur* and *Mercury* in love, then it brings itself forth higher than it is in its current degree. Just as the Eternal Liberty, with its <term>Lubet</term> <note>Divine longing, delight, or inclination.</note>, introduces Eternal Nature through mortification into desire and thereby brings itself forth higher—namely, in power and majesty—the same is to be considered in all things. For all things arise out of one single Being. This same Being is a mystery of all beings, and a manifestation of the <term>Abyss in Byss</term> <note>The manifestation of the bottomless, infinite void (Abyss) into a grounded, tangible state (Byss).</note>.

<summary>Böhme explains that true healing and spiritual perfection require "mortification"—a process where the fundamental elements of a thing die to their corrupt state to be reborn in a higher, purified form. He argues that raw medicines only treat symptoms, while true alchemical transformation reaches the "root" or center of the life-form.</summary>

75. All things are generated out of the Grand Mystery <term>original: *mysterium magnum*; in Böhme's philosophy, the chaotic or potential source of all things</term>, and proceed from one degree into another. Now, whatever goes forward in its own degree receives no abomination <note>original: Abominate; a state of corruption, disharmony, or "unnaturalness"</note>, whether it be in vegetables or animals. But whatever enters into itself—into its own self-hood, namely into its own desire <term>original: *Lubet*; the innate divine inclination or "pleasure" of the spirit</term>—the same receives the abomination while passing through the degrees. For each form of nature <margin>Or proceeding from.</margin> out of the Mystery receives its own property in its hunger, and therein it is not annoyed or molested, for it is part of their own property.

76. But if the will turns back again into the birth of the other properties, then it receives a craving <note>original: Lust; a specific inclination or misplaced desire</note>, and that craving creates a hunger, and the hunger receives a foreign essence into itself. Here, then, the abomination and the turmoil <term>original: *Turba*; the destructive awakening of the wrathful property in nature</term> are born. For this will has entered, contrary to the course of nature, into a foreign essence which is not its own property. This foreign essence now dominates the foreign will and overcomes it. Now the will must either <margin>Text: spew out.</margin> spew it out, or else it will itself be cast out by the foreign essence; and since this also cannot be, anger and enmity arise from it.

77. For the properties run to their center of the first impression <term>the original "contraction" or desire that gives form to matter</term> and seek the strength and power of the fire. From this arises heat and cold in the body, and they exist within one another as enemies. By this, the "first mother" <note>the generative power of nature</note> is stirred up in her most wrathful malice and malignity according to the harsh impression. Then begins the contest for victory, and that property which maintains its power and prevalence casts the other into the property of death—namely, into destruction <note>original: Devoration</note>, into the house of misery.

# The Fifteenth Chapter.

### *Concerning the Will of the great Mystery in Good and Evil, showing from where a good and evil Will arises, and how one introduces itself into the other.*

1. EVERY property takes its origin from the first—namely, from the first impression or desire toward nature, out of the Grand Mystery—and brings itself forth out of itself, just as the air proceeds out of the fire. All that proceeds forward in one will is uncontrollable <note>cannot be hindered or diverted from its path</note>, for it gives itself to no other property; it dwells even from its first origin only in itself and goes forth in one will. This is the true way of eternity, wherein there is no corruptibility if a thing remains in its own peculiar property, for the Grand Mystery is from eternity. Now, if the form of the same proceeds forth and manifests itself out of itself, then this form stands with its root in the mystery of eternity. But if the form brings itself forth into another craving <note>original: Lust</note>, so that two properties must dwell in one, then enmity and abomination arise from that. For from eternity there has been only the one element in <margin>Or working property.</margin> *motion*, and the free desire <term>Lubet</term> of eternity, which proceeded forth with its motion from the Grand Mystery of eternity as a spirit, which spirit is God’s.

2. But when the Grand Mystery once moved itself and introduced the free desire <note>Lubet</note> into the desire for essence, then the strife began within that desire. For there arose in the desire out of the element (which bears only one will) four elements—namely, manifold desires and wills which rule in only one body, where there is now contrariety <note>opposition or conflict</note>...

<summary>This page explains Jacob Böhme's cosmological view on how disharmony and "abomination" arise when a natural property turns away from its own essence to crave a foreign one. It details the transition from the singular, eternal element into the conflicting four elements and the resulting struggle between properties.</summary>
<keywords>Grand Mystery, Jacob Böhme, Lubet, Turba, four elements, spiritual alchemy, origin of evil, properties of nature, desire, essence</keywords>

--- Page 409 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's philosophical exploration of the "Self-will" versus the "Divine Will," specifically focusing on how the four elements create internal conflict within man and how "Resignation" (surrender to God) is the only path to peace.</meta>

<page-num>124</page-num>
# The Signature of All Things: Chapter 15

...and strife; just as heat opposes cold, fire opposes water, and air opposes earth, each is the death and destruction of the other. Thus, the creature existing in this state is nothing but a continual dying and a struggle. It is an enmity and a contrary will within itself, which cannot be cured unless it enters again into one single Will. This cannot happen unless the multiplicity of wills is destroyed and dies completely to the desire from which the four elements arise, so that the will again becomes what it was from eternity. In this, we humans recognize what we are within the rule <margin>We are our own enemies.</margin> of the four elements: nothing but a conflict and a contrary will, a <gloss>original: "self-envying"</gloss> self-resentment, a desire for what is loathsome <note>original: "Abominate" - things that are unnatural or contrary to the divine order</note>, and a craving for death.

3. For the lust that arises out of desire must die. If the will—which came from the great Mystery of Eternity and was breathed by the Spirit of God into the image of man (that is, into His likeness)—is to be freed from the loathsome and contrary will, then the desire of the four elements must die. The will must enter again into the one only element; it must once more receive its eternal right and act within that single element, just as God created man. Man opposed this state and brought himself under the power of the four elements, where he inherited death and conflict within the forms of life. From this arise his sickness, loathing, and enmity. For everything that lives in God’s will has not risen in "self-will"; or, if it has risen there, it has died again to its own [or *selfish*] desire.

4. Every will that enters into its "self-hood" <term>Self-hood: Böhme’s term for the ego-centered state of being separated from God</term> and seeks the basis of its own life-form breaks itself off from the Great Mystery. It enters into a self-centeredness, wanting to be its own master [or within its own *selfish* jurisdiction], and so it is contrary to the first Mystery, for that Mystery alone is everything. This "child" is considered evil because it struggles in disobedience against its own mother who gave it birth. But if the child again directs its will and desire back into that from which it was originally generated and born, then it is completely one with it and cannot be harmed by anything; for it enters into the "nothing"—that is, into the essence from which it first came.

5. Therefore, O man! Understand what you must do; look at yourself within yourself to see what you are. See whether or not you stand in the resignation <term>Resignation: the spiritual practice of surrendering the individual will to the Divine Will</term> of your Mother (out of whom you were generated and created in the beginning), and whether you are inclined toward that same will. If not, then know that you are a rebellious, stubborn, and disobedient child. You have made yourself your own enemy because you have entered into self-desire and self-will. You have made yourself your own selfish possession, so that you cannot dwell in the first Mother, but only in yourself. For your will has entered into "self-hood"; all that vexes, plagues, and annoys you is only your own self-hood. You make yourself your own enemy and bring yourself to self-destruction or death.

6. Now, if you wish to escape death, you must completely forsake your own self-desire, which has introduced itself into a foreign essence and become self-centered. In your self-hood and self-desire, you must become as "nothing," so that you no longer will or desire anything for yourself. Instead, you must wholly and fully turn your desire back, through resignation, into the eternal—that is, into God’s will—so that His will may be your will and desire.

7. Without this, there is nothing but misery and death—a continual dying and perishing. This is where the Election of Grace <note>The theological concept of God's sovereign choice to redeem humanity through mercy</note> arises. If the human will—which departed from the unity of eternity and entered into self-centeredness (that is, into a selfish lust and desire)—again breaks away from self-hood and enters into the mortification <note>The "death" or subduing of the selfish nature</note> of the self-will, and turns its desire back only toward the first Mother, then the first Mother chooses it again to be her child. She makes it one again with the only will of eternity. But the person who continues in self-hood continues in eternal death—that is, in an eternal, selfish enmity. This alone is called "sin": it is an enmity against God, because the creature insists on being under its own selfish command and government.

<summary>Böhme argues that human suffering and sin stem from "self-hood," a state where the individual will separates from God's eternal unity to pursue selfish desires. He concludes that true salvation and the "Election of Grace" are found only when a person surrenders their self-will and returns to the divine source.</summary>
<keywords>Jakob Böhme, Signatura Rerum, Self-hood, Resignation, Four Elements, Divine Will, Election of Grace, Sin, Ego, Spiritual Rebirth</keywords>

# Chap. 15. The Signature of all Things.

8. Thus, in its *self-centeredness*—that is, in a *dominion* full of *contention* and *strife*—it cannot either will or do anything that is good. Just as it imposes, awakens, and powerfully stirs up nothing but *dying* and *death* within *itself*, it can do nothing else for its *fellow members*. From this also arises falsehood <note>original: "Falshood [or Lyes]"</note>, because the *creature* denies its *union* with <note>original: "with [or in]"</note> the *will of God* and puts its own *self-centeredness* in that *place*. Thus, it departs from *unity* into *desires* and *self-lusts*. If it truly knew that all *beings* were its *mothers* which brought it forth, and did not hold the *mother's substance* as its own but as common to all, then *covetousness, envy, strife*, and a contrary *will* and *enmity* would not arise—from which the *anger* (that is, the *fire of destruction*) originates.

9. All *sins* arise from the *self*; for *self-centeredness* forces itself through *desire* into its own *self-fulfillment*. It creates in itself *covetousness* and *envy*; it draws *strange essences* <note>foreign or external influences and desires</note> into itself through its own *desire*, and also turns the *possessor* of those *strange essences* into an *enemy* against itself. Thus, *sin* is built upon *sin*, and *vileness* upon *vileness*, and all run confusedly in and among one another as a mere *abomination* before the *Eternal Mother*.

10. In the same way, we must also consider the *regenerated will*, which leaves its *selfishness* or *self-centeredness* and returns to *resignation* <note>original: "Resignation"; in this context, it refers to the act of yielding or surrendering one's will to God</note>. This will also becomes an *enemy* and an *abomination* to *self-centeredness*, just as *sickness* is an *enemy* to *health*, and conversely, *health* is an *enemy* to *sickness*. Thus, the *resigned will* and the *self-will* are in *continual enmity* and an *incessant, lasting war* and *combat*.

11. *Self-will* seeks only what serves its own *self-centeredness*, but the *resigned will* is not at all anxious. Instead, it brings its *desire* only into its *Eternal Mother*, so that it might be one with her. *It desires to be a "nothing,"* so that the *Mother* might be everything within it. *Self-will* says to the *resigned will*, "*You are foolish* to give yourself over to *death* when you might live gloriously in me." But the *resigned will* says, "*You are my abomination, pain, and enmity. You bring me out of eternity into time, and only into perplexity and misery; you plague me for a while, and then you give my body to the earth and my soul to hell.*"

12. *True, real resignation* is the *mortification* <note>original: "Mortification"; the spiritual practice of "killing off" the sinful nature or worldly desires</note> of that which is *abominable* to *God*. He who wholly forsakes his *self-centeredness* and gives himself up—with *mind* and *desire, senses* and *will*—into *God’s mercy* and into the *dying of Jesus Christ*, is dead to the *earthly world* in his *will*. He is a *two-fold man*: one part is the *abomination* which works only within itself toward *death*, but the *resigned will* lives in *Christ’s death* and rises up continually in *Christ’s resurrection* in *God*. And though the *self-desire* sins—which indeed can do nothing else but sin—the *resigned will* does not live in *sin*, for it is dead to the *desire of sin*. It lives through *Christ* in *God* in the *land of the living*, while *self-centeredness* lives in the *land of death*—that is, in *continual dying* and *continual enmity* against *God*.

13. The *earthly man* is the *curse of God* and is an *abomination* before *God’s holiness*; he can do nothing else but seek his own *self-interest*, for he exists within the *wrath of God*. Even if he does something good, he does it not from his own *self-will*, but because the *will resigned in God* compels him to do what his *self* would not willingly do. And if he does it, he does it as an *instrument* of the *resigned will*, not from his own *desire*, but from *God’s will*, which guides the *resigned will* in its *desire* as an *instrument*.

14. Therefore, whoever wishes to see the *Kingdom of God* and attain it must *draw out* <note>original: "educe"</note> his *soul* from *self-centeredness* and from *earthly desire*. It is like a *physician* who extracts the *cure* for a *disease* from a *painful* <note>original: "tormenting"</note> *desire* and introduces it into a *love-desire*. Then the *cure* also draws the *sickness* in the *body* out of the *painful desire* and places it into a *love-desire*. *Sickness* thus becomes the *servant* of the *medicine*; and likewise, the evil *earthly will*, once the *soul’s will* is cured, becomes the *servant of the resigned will*.

<summary>Boehme describes the spiritual conflict between the self-centered ego ("Self-hood") and the surrendered soul ("Resignation"), arguing that true spiritual life requires the death of the selfish will so that God's will can act through the person. He concludes with a medical metaphor, likening the process of spiritual salvation to a physician transforming a painful disease into a state of health.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Chapter 15 of Signatura Rerum, discussing the struggle between the "resigned Will" (the soul surrendered to God) and "Self-hood" (the egoistic, earthly nature).</meta>

### Signatura Rerum: Chapter 15

15. The physical and astral <term>original: "elemental and siderial"</term> human must only be the instrument with which a person’s soul works in a state of yieldedness <note>The "resigned Will" (German: Gelassenheit) is a central concept for Boehme, referring to the soul surrendering its own ego to God's will.</note>; for God has created it for that purpose. However, in the person of Adam, the soul has established itself as lord and master; it has entered into the prison of the world and surrendered its will to it. But if the soul is to be recognized as God’s child, it must die to that worldly nature again. It must be completely mortified <note>put to death or subdued</note> to earthly selfishness and desire through God's will in the death of Christ. It must be entirely born again in God's will, depriving the earthly ego of its power, ruling over it, and commanding it as a master directs his instrument. Then, selfishness loses its power and dominance, and the lust of the ego remains only as a persistent craving. Selfishness then continually longs after the forms of its own life—namely, self-glory and earthly abundance, as well as envy and anger (to see if it might attain that abundance), and the cunning lies of falsehood. These are the vital forms of the earthly ego.

16. But the resigned Will, like a powerful champion, continually bruises the head of this serpent and says, "You have arisen from the Devil and God's anger; I will have nothing to do with you, for you are an abomination before God." And even though the resigned Will is sometimes captured by false lusts—when the Devil’s desires and the insinuations of his imagination overwhelm it—the resigned Will immediately cries out to <margin>a Voice or Breath.</margin> the Word of God, so that God’s will may bring it out of the abomination of death.

17. The resigned Will has no rest here in this "cottage" <note>a metaphor for the physical body</note>, but must always be in combat, for it is lodged in a false house. In itself, it is indeed in God’s hand; but outside of itself, it is in the jaws and throat of the abyss of God’s anger in the kingdom of devils. These devils continually pass back and forth around it, desiring to test and tempt the soul—that is, the center of the being.

18. In the same way, the good angels also stand by the person who remains in the resigned Will (the Divine Desire) and defend him from the poisonous imagination of the Devil; they keep off the "fiery darts of the wicked one," as St. Peter says.

19. For everyone works and desires within the context of God's love and His anger. While a person is in this "tabernacle" <note>the mortal body</note>, he stands at a gate, ready to go either out or in. Both eternal principles <note>the light/love of God and the dark/wrath of God</note> are active within him. Whichever one the soul’s will gives itself to, by that principle it is received and chosen. He is pulled by both, and if the soul's will remains in selfishness, then he is in the hand of God’s anger.

20. But if he departs from his selfishness and forsakes his own damnation—continually throwing himself only into God’s mercy (namely, into the suffering, death, resurrection, and restoration of Christ) and willing nothing for himself except what God wills in and through him—then the will is dead to the life and desire of God's anger. This is because it has no life of its own, but lies in the death of selfishness and the desire of the Devil. The anger of God cannot reach him, for he is as "nothing," and yet he is in God. He lives entirely in the Divine Essence, but not for himself; he lives for his first "Mother of Eternity" <note>the divine source or wisdom from which the soul originated</note>. He is back in the place where he was before he was a creature, in the same Will in which God created him. He is an instrument in the voice of God, upon which only the Will-Spirit of God strikes, for His own honor and for deeds of wonder.

21. All self-centered seeking and searching within the ego is a vain thing. The "self-will" understands nothing of God, for it is not *in* God, but outside of Him in its own selfishness. However, the resigned Will understands God. It does not do this by its own power, but through the Spirit in whom it stands still; the Spirit, whose instrument the will is, manifests Himself in the Divine Voice within it as much as He pleases. And although a person may learn much through his ego by searching and study (which is not entirely useless), his understanding remains only on the outside, in the "expressed Word" <note>The physical, created world or the literal text</note>—that is, in the form of the letter. He understands nothing of the inner form of the—
